findings.title: The bare sequencer ingress (sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com) is a separate, non-Cloudflare endpoint in us-east-2 that accepts only eth_sendRawTransaction
findings.claim: Robinhood's connecting page lists three distinct hosts: rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com (public RPC), feed.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com (feed) and sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com (sequencer). Probed today from this box: rpc.* and feed.* resolve to customer-origin.offchainlabs.com on Cloudflare (2606:4700::, cf-ray IAD; rpc returned 429 on a handful of eth_calls, feed returned 403 with retry-after 1978 s), whereas sequencer.* is a CNAME to ac23019b22f1ae5a-sequencer.ue2v1.rhm.arbitrum-internal.io with three AWS us-east-2 A records (3.136.74.196, 3.141.111.43, 3.142.9.34), served by istio-envoy over HTTP/2, and it rejects eth_chainId/eth_blockNumber/net_version ('method does not exist/is not available') while eth_sendRawTransaction is wired ('missing value for required argument 0'). BlockRazor's benchmark also names https://sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com as 'the official sequencer endpoint' and Robinhood docs say the public RPC is rate-limited and not for latency-sensitive use.
findings.relevance: Sequencer reply latency (100 ms median, up to 4 s) and first-vs-second landing (9 points). If the engine submits via rpc.* or a provider, every shot crosses a Cloudflare edge and a rate limiter before reaching the Nitro sequencer; the three sequencer IPs are almost certainly one NLB listener per AZ, so one of them is same-AZ with our c7a.large (~0.1-0.3 ms) and the other two are cross-AZ (~0.5-1 ms).
findings.test: From the c7a.large: (1) confirm which host the engine's sendRawTransaction actually hits; (2) measure TCP-connect RTT to each of the three IPs 200 times and pin the lowest with --resolve; (3) A/B 100 same-nonce pairs (one via the current path, one via the pinned sequencer IP over a pre-warmed HTTP/2 connection) and count which lands first and the reply latency distribution; (4) read our zone id from IMDS (/latest/meta-data/placement/availability-zone-id) so the AZ mapping is explicit.

findings.title: Sequencer is in AWS us-east-2 on Offchain Labs' RaaS, and the public feed's lag inside Ohio is 27-97 ms p50 / 85-953 ms p99 depending on AZ (use2-az2 is the bad one)
findings.claim: The sequencer CNAME 'ue2v1.rhm.arbitrum-internal.io' and Glassnode's probe page both place the sequencer in AWS us-east-2 (Ohio). BlockRazor measured the official feed (feed.mainnet, Cloudflare-fronted) against its node-direct feed on 13,251 blocks on 10 Sep 2026 from the three Ohio zones: use2-az1 p50 28.0 ms / p99 85.8 ms behind; use2-az3 p50 27.3 ms / p99 111.7 ms; use2-az2 p50 97.4 ms / p99 953.1 ms / max 1,616 ms. The chainstack decoder README adds: the feed is rate-limited per client (not per connection), a fresh connection replays ~124 s (1,203 messages) of backlog unless you send the Arbitrum-Requested-Sequence-Number header, and there is a separate delayed-feed host ~500 ms behind.
findings.relevance: The 2-fleet gate is computed from blocks seen before the E1 tick and the burst is aimed relative to feed-observed block phase. With p50 lag of 1/4 to 1 block and p99 of 1-9 blocks, the gate under-counts fleets in the last blocks before the tick and the phase estimate jitters; being in use2-az2 would make this roughly 3x worse. 'Launches whose crowd appears only in the tick's own block cannot be taken' may partly be feed lag rather than true absence.
findings.test: Log feed message arrival time minus (previous arrival + 100 ms) for a day and report p50/p99 by hour; compare fleet counts computed live at decision time vs recomputed post-hoc from the full feed for the same launches (how many launches flip across the 2-fleet threshold); read our zone id; if we are in use2-az2 or p99 lag > 100 ms, launch a second c7a.large in use2-az1/az3 and repeat. Always reconnect with the sequence-number header and keep one feed client per IP.

findings.title: Nitro block-building rules verified on this chain: 32M gas per block, 95 KB calldata per block, arrival-order retry queue, 1024-slot submit queue with 12 s timeout, and blocks-per-second is not fixed at 10
findings.claim: ArbGasInfo.getGasAccountingParams() on chain 4663 returns speedLimitPerSecond = 7,000,000, gasPoolMax = 32,000,000, maxTxGasLimit = 32,000,000 (so the per-block gas cap is 32M, same as Arbitrum One); Arbitrum docs state a block also closes at 95,000 bytes of calldata. In sequencer.go, a tx that does not fit gets core.ErrGasLimitReached and is pushed to txRetryQueue, which is drained first in the next block (FCFS is preserved across block boundaries); publishTransactionToQueue blocks on a 1024-slot channel until queue-timeout (default 12 s); eth_sendRawTransaction only returns after the tx has been executed in a block (queueItem.returnResult). Sampling 1,500 consecutive blocks today (09:15 UTC, a quiet hour) via publicnode: max gasUsed 10.1M, max 73 txs, max block size 75,965 bytes, ~160k gas per tx in the busiest blocks; blocks per timestamp-second were 10 in 137 of 151 seconds but 6, 9 and 19 in the others (Arbitrum docs: under load the sequencer produces blocks faster than nominal).
findings.relevance: Explains 'under crowds of 400+ rival shots the sequencer holds our burst for seconds and we miss': at ~160k gas per buy attempt the E1 block holds at most ~200 attempts by gas (or ~250-300 by bytes), so a 400+ crowd necessarily spills into 2-3 blocks and the serial execution of 32M-gas blocks takes hundreds of ms each. It also changes the model of the E1 race: everything that arrives between the cut of the last E0 block and the cut of the first E1 block lands in the E1 block in arrival order, so the top slot goes to the fleet whose first shot arrived earliest after the previous block was cut, not to whoever is closest to the second boundary; a burst starting only 46 ms before the boundary can be first only when the previous block was cut inside that 46 ms window (consistent with ~60% first). And 'hold 11 blocks' is 0.6-1.8 s of wall time, not 1.1 s.
findings.test: From our feed archive and receipts: for each fill compute our first shot's index in its block, the number of rival buy attempts ahead of us, the block's gasUsed and size vs the 32M/95 KB caps, and our send time relative to the arrival of the previous block. If rivals ahead of us were sent before our -46 ms start, simulate starting the burst one full block earlier (~-110 ms) and keeping 2 ms spacing; cost is only the extra BuyOnce no-ops (~30-50k gas each at today's 0.02 gwei floor = $0.003, or ~$0.06 at the Sep-3 0.5 gwei peak). Separately, re-express the 11-block hold in seconds using actual block timestamps and check whether the sell realized differently in seconds with 19 blocks/s.

findings.title: The tax schedule is owner-mutable and has already been changed once: docs say 5 s, source default 15 s, live factory says 3 s; a change to 2 s or back to 5 s flips the E1 seat
findings.claim: Live reads today on the V2 factory 0x7eD598BcEf8bd9Edd8C97A195C6d13f40801EC7e (confirmed as the factory by Bitquery's Pons API docs and docs.ponsfamily.com): snipeTaxStartBps() = 9900, snipeTaxSeconds() = 3, maxCreatorTaxBps() = 1000, launchFee() = 0.0005 ETH, owner() = 0x263ed295dafae1d9aadd6e56c4b6f9f38ee019dd. The official docs describe a 5-second decay ('about 25% at 1 s, ~3% at 2 s'), and the public source defaults to 15 s; the decay formula that reproduces our measured 99% / 6.18% / 0.19% is bps = 9900 >> ((elapsed_seconds * 14) / snipeTaxSeconds). Setters setSnipeTaxSeconds (0xd1ec471a) and setSnipeTaxStartBps (0xb20e51af) are onlyOwner with caps MAX_SNIPE_TAX_SECONDS = 60 and MAX_SNIPE_TAX_START_BPS = 9900; exemption list max 32 addresses, fixed at creation, launcher and creator-fee recipient auto-exempt; fee caps curve <= 10%, creator tax <= 10%, total <= 20%. Issue #10 shows the published curve source lacks the snipe-tax code, so deployed bytecode differs from the repo. Arithmetic: seconds = 5 gives E1 = 24.75%; seconds = 2 gives E1 = 9900 >> 7 = 0.77%; seconds = 4 gives E1 = 9900 >> 3 = 12.4%.
findings.relevance: Fees take 36% of the gross move and the whole seat model (E1 = 6.18%) rests on one owner-settable integer that has already moved from 5 to 3. A move to 2 s would make E1 nearly free (and crowd it); a move back to 5 s would make every E1 fill a loser before the guard even fires.
findings.test: Poll snipeTaxSeconds() and snipeTaxStartBps() on the factory once per block from the feed (or watch feed calldata for selectors 0xd1ec471a / 0xb20e51af from the owner) and recompute the seat table and a kill-switch automatically; backfill the factory's call history to date the 5-to-3 change (Blockscout is Cloudflare-gated from datacenter IPs; use robinscan.io or Bitquery's Calls cube) and check whether our Sep 21-29 backtest window straddles it.

findings.title: Venue supply is collapsing on independent data: Pons daily fees fell 47% from the Sep 21-23 window to Sep 26-28 and 88% from the Sep 5 peak; launches ~36k/day peak to ~6k; the 90-day Robinhood-Wallet gas subsidy ended Sep 29
findings.claim: DefiLlama daily Pons fees (USD): Sep 5 11,418,716 (peak); Sep 14 5,347,714; Sep 21 3,389,265; Sep 22 2,580,573; Sep 23 2,444,706; Sep 24 1,817,273; Sep 25 1,608,949; Sep 26 1,680,957; Sep 27 1,310,993; Sep 28 1,461,061; Sep 29 (partial) 1,338,354. Robinhood Chain gas fees: Sep 9 $1.055M -> Sep 27 $68k, Sep 28 $108k. AMBCrypto (Sep 28): daily launches ~36,000 at peak to ~6,000; PONS buybacks from >$1M/day to ~$200k. findings.test: Regress daily fireable-launch count (Sep 21-29) on DefiLlama daily Pons fees; use the fitted ratio as a daily fill-budget forecast and as the regime switch; compare Sep 29-Oct 2 against the fit to quantify the post-subsidy step.

findings.title: Timeboost / express lane is confirmed off on Robinhood Chain (feed messages carry no express-lane bitmap); ordering is strict arrival order at the sequencer
findings.claim: chainstack's decoder README: the blockMetadata field that carries Timeboost's express-lane bitmap on every Arbitrum One message is absent on Robinhood Chain, 'no express lane, no bidding'. L2BEAT lists a single Robinhood sequencer/batch poster (0xDaa5...87F4, ArbOS 61) with no Timeboost. Robinhood docs: 'order is determined strictly by the arrival time at the sequencer; no transaction can bypass others by paying higher fees' (PumpDev measured median tips ~0.02 gwei, i.e. nobody pays for priority). crypto.news notes Timeboost adoption is a 'live question' because its MEV revenue would fall under the 10% Arbitrum DAO share (Robinhood has paid ~$200k on $2M+ revenue).
findings.relevance: Confirms there is nothing to buy: the 9-point first-vs-second gap can only be closed by arrival time. It is also the one venue change that would end the E1 game overnight (express-lane controller gets a 200 ms head start per round).
findings.test: Add a watchdog on the feed that alerts when blockMetadata becomes non-empty or when an ExpressLaneAuction contract appears; no action otherwise.

findings.title: BlockRazor's Ohio benchmark shows the official submission path is beatable even in-region: 60.46% same-nonce wins over 703 rounds; their node-direct feed is 0 ms vs 27-97 ms for the public feed
findings.claim: Vendor benchmark (Sep 10, 2026): from Ohio, 703 same-nonce pairs sent simultaneously to BlockRazor's Ohio endpoint and to the official sequencer endpoint -> BlockRazor first 60.46%; 703 distinct-nonce rounds -> earlier block/index 54.62%. From Frankfurt/Singapore/Tokyo 65-70%. Feed: node-required Ultra feed 0.000 ms at all percentiles vs official feed p50 27-97 ms; priced $200/day or $2,000/month; tx-sending endpoints exist in Frankfurt, Ohio, Singapore, Tokyo, pricing not published, 'create an account and start for free'. Their feed URLs: wss://us.robinhood-feeder.blockrazor.io/ws/ultra/{token} and jp.*.
findings.relevance: First-vs-second landing (60% live). If a third party wins 60/40 against the official ingress from the same region, the official path has several ms of removable jitter; that is exactly the margin between first and second in a 2 ms-spaced burst. At $13 stakes the paid feed is not justifiable, but a free trial of tx-sending is a cheap experiment and the same-nonce A/B is the right measurement method regardless.
findings.test: Open a free account, get the Ohio tx-sending endpoint, and run our own 100-pair same-nonce A/B against the pinned sequencer IP; expected value = (delta first-landing rate) x 9 points x fills/day; adopt only if the delta survives 200 pairs and the price is below that.

findings.title: Robinhood's ArbOS 61 compliance filter voids transactions after sequencing (status 0x0, no logs, gas burned): ~150 per day chain-wide, no published criteria
findings.claim: An authorized filterer (0xebDc18A1...24b7) registers tx hashes in the ArbFilteredTransactionsManager precompile (0x...74); the state transition then forcibly fails those transactions, which still appear in blocks with status 0x0 and gas fully burned; 6,092 filtered in the first six weeks (~150/day), active since 30 Jun 2026 14:53 UTC. L2BEAT flags the count rising from 278 to 6,086 by July. chainstack's rhfeed exposes is_filtered_call(tx_hash) to test a hash against the precompile.
findings.relevance: A silent miss mode: a voided shot looks like an ordinary revert in our receipts. If a relay contract or a burst of 35 near-identical transactions from 35 wallets ever matches whatever heuristic the filterer uses, fills disappear without any error from the sequencer.
findings.test: For every landed shot with status 0 in the live log since Sep 26, call the precompile (or rhfeed.is_filtered_call) with the tx hash and count matches; add the check to the post-fill audit so a filtered shot is classified separately from a guard revert.

findings.title: Every public Pons sniper (bodkin, dzo, loxley, Trustdev, PumpDev API) waits for tax <= 300 bps or 19 bps and enters 1.1-2.1 s after detection; none play E1, so the E1 competitors are private fleets and the public bots are the E2/E3 wave we sell into
findings.claim: bodkin and dzo poll currentSnipeTaxBps(address) every 150 ms and fire at 0.18-0.31% tax, measured 1.1-2.1 s after websocket detection; loxley fires below a 300 bps ceiling; the Trustdev bot 'rejects blind first-block buy'; PumpDev's hosted trade API builds a tx in ~200 ms and enforces amountOutMin from recent trades. Their shared exits: +80% take-profit, -35% stop, 25% trailing, 45-min max hold, 'DEV SOLD' trigger on deployer CurveSell. Public-RPC capacity they report: 8 parallel calls OK, 16 -> ~50% rejected, batch of 12 rejected. 24h stats they logged for Sep 3: 24,462 launches / 559 graduations.
findings.relevance: Our 11-block hold sells ~1.1 s after the E1 block, i.e. ~2.1 s after creation, which is exactly when this cohort's buys land (E2/E3); their -35% stops and dev-sold triggers are the sell pressure that follows. Explains why the 11-block exit tested best and gives an external prior for what the E2/E3 flow looks like.
findings.test: From the feed, for each of the 130 modelled fills count E2 and E3 buy attempts and their total quote size, and check the correlation with our realized exit; if E2+E3 size predicts exit quality, it is a free post-entry sizing signal for the sell (split sell vs single sell at block 11), not a new gate.

findings.title: Exempt-bundle rug launches (53 launches, $18.4M, Jul 10-Sep 21) dump 'one second after launch', i.e. at E1; the exemption list is visible in the creation calldata
findings.claim: Wazz (@WazzCrypto, Sep 27) and The Block: one operation ran 53 launches; creators exempted 15-25 wallets, one transaction 1-3 blocks after creation bought for all of them (emptying the curve into Uniswap v4), creators and exempt wallets kept 82-86% of supply, and 'sellers began moving tokens one second after launch'; 25 of the 53 used one unverified 'commercial bundling tool' contract created Aug 28. The exemption list is an explicit argument of launchToken(..., address[] snipeTaxExemptions) / launchTokenFor(..., originalDeployer, address[] snipeTaxExemptions), so its length is decodable from the TokenLaunched transaction's calldata on the feed before the E1 tick. No Pons or Robinhood countermeasure has been announced.
findings.relevance: An E1 buyer is the designated exit liquidity for these launches; they also produce large, visible 'crowds' (exempt buys at second 0 plus fleets chasing them), which may be what the 2-fleet gate is selecting for. This is new external evidence on which launches to skip, not a re-proposal of the nine rejected signals unless one of them was already 'exemption-list length'.
findings.test: Decode snipeTaxExemptions length and the launchTokenFor forwarder address from the creation tx for the 696 qualifying launches; split the 130 modelled fills by list length (0 / 1-5 / 6+) and by use of the Aug-28 bundler contract and compare realized outcome and guard-miss rate.

findings.title: Gas is not a hidden cost at today's floor, but it was 25x higher three weeks ago: base fee 0.02 gwei now (floor) vs 0.511 gwei on Sep 3; block gas price responds to sustained load above 7M gas/s
findings.claim: Bitquery: base fee 0.02 gwei on Aug 22 to 0.511 gwei on Sep 3 (25x); median swap fee $0.012 to $0.48; the chain ran at ~40M gas/s against a 7M gas/s speed limit (getGasAccountingParams confirms speedLimitPerSecond = 7,000,000, pricing inertia 102, backlog tolerance 10). Today's latest block shows baseFeePerGas 0.020078 gwei and gas backlog 0. PumpDev reports median tips ~0.02 gwei and a 100 gwei priority-fee ceiling (tips buy nothing under FCFS).
findings.relevance: Cost per fill: a 35-shot burst with 34 no-ops at ~30-50k gas each is ~$0.003 per no-op now but was ~$0.06-0.10 per no-op (up to ~$3 per burst, 25% of a $13 stake) during the Sep 3 regime; the model's linear capacity to $200 should include gas by regime, and any decision to widen the burst (finding 3) must be priced at the crowd-time base fee, which rises precisely when crowds are 400+.
findings.test: Join each live burst's 35 receipts to baseFeePerGas and compute realized gas per fill as a percent of stake, split by crowd size; add ArbGasInfo.getGasBacklog() (0x1d5b5c20) to the per-launch telemetry so gas cost is forecast before the burst rather than after.

findings.title: Submit to the documented direct sequencer host (Envoy, HTTP/2, no Cloudflare), not the Cloudflare-fronted public RPC
findings.claim: Robinhood documents a dedicated sequencer endpoint, https://sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com (plus wss://feed.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com and a delayed backup feed ~500 ms behind). Probed today: the sequencer host answers with 'server: istio-envoy', negotiates HTTP/2, has no Cloudflare headers, and exposes only eth_sendRawTransaction and eth_sendRawTransactionConditional (eth_chainId/eth_call return -32601). The public https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com is behind Cloudflare (cf-ray, server: cloudflare) and its sendRawTransaction is relayed by a full node's forwarder; nitro's DefaultNodeForwarderConfig keeps MaxIdleConnections=1 to the sequencer, so a 35-shot burst through the RPC path opens fresh connections under load. Glassnode places the sequencer in AWS us-east-2 (Ohio) with ~3 ms submit RTT from Ohio vs 140 ms Tokyo. Neither host accepts a WebSocket upgrade (HTTP 400).
findings.relevance: Landing second on ~40% of fills and the 'sequencer holds our burst for seconds under 400+ shots' both depend on the ingress path. If any shot goes through the Cloudflare RPC or a third-party RPC, it carries extra hops plus the forwarder's single idle connection; the direct Envoy host with pre-warmed HTTP/2 streams removes them.
findings.test: Same-nonce pair races (BlockRazor's method: 50+ pairs, identical nonce, different recipient per path) from the c7a.large between the direct host and the current path; also curl -w timings (connect/TLS/first-byte) to the direct host from us-east-2a/b/c micro-instances to pick the AZ with the lowest RTT.

findings.title: Never JSON-RPC-batch the burst: nitro's sendRawTransaction blocks until sequenced and geth batches run sequentially
findings.claim: In nitro, PublishTransaction pushes the tx into txQueue and then waits on resultChan, which is only fulfilled after the tx is included in a block (queue-timeout 12 s, abort deadline 24 s). That is why the measured 'reply' is ~100 ms median: it is inclusion latency, not network RTT. geth's handleBatch processes the elements of a JSON-RPC batch one at a time in a single goroutine (msg := callBuffer.nextCall(); resp := h.handleCallMsg(cp, msg)), whereas each single-message call gets its own goroutine via startCallProc. A batch of 35 sendRawTransaction calls therefore serializes 35 inclusion waits (blocks apart). Over HTTP/1.1 one in-flight request per connection applies, so 35 concurrent shots need 35 keep-alive connections or HTTP/2 multiplexing (the Envoy sequencer host negotiates h2).
findings.relevance: Shot spacing of 2 ms is only real if every shot is an independent request on its own connection/stream; any batching or connection-pool cap (e.g. an HTTP client limited to 10 connections per host) silently turns the burst into a queue and costs first place.
findings.test: Inspect the client transport (max connections per host, h2 enabled, pre-warmed TLS) and check block positions of the 35 shots on a dry launch: they should occupy contiguous positions; a gap of a whole block between shots indicates serialization.

findings.title: Exact E1 block composition rule from nitro source: retry queue first, then arrival order; overflow triggers are 32M gas or 95,000 bytes per block
findings.claim: createBlock waits for the first queued tx, then drains txQueue non-blockingly for at most ReadFromTxQueueTimeout (10 ms default), then takes the block timestamp with time.Now().Unix() AFTER the drain, and the loop re-arms at nextBlock = callTime + MaxBlockSpeed (RH chain: measured exactly 10 blocks per second over 61 consecutive blocks 75543052-75543112). Items are taken from txRetryQueue before txQueue; txRetryQueue holds transactions that failed the previous block with ErrGasLimitReached, which happens when blockGasLeft < 21000 (ArbOS >= 50 counts gas actually used; RH runs ArbOS 61, PerBlockGasLimit measured via ArbGasInfo.getGasAccountingParams = 32,000,000, speed limit 7,000,000 gas/s) or when the block's summed raw tx bytes exceed MaxTxDataSize (95,000 bytes default). At drain time any tx whose maxFeePerGas is below the last block's baseFee is dropped (ErrFeeCapTooLow); RH base fee floats around 20.0-20.4e6 wei. Held nonce-too-high txs (1 s cache) are re-inserted directly after their predecessor by precheckNonces, not at the head.
findings.relevance: Explains the 400+ crowd failure: 400 shots x ~250 bytes exceeds 95 KB, so the last block of the creation second overflows and its overflow leads the E1 block regardless of who arrives first after the boundary; such launches are structurally unwinnable by arrival timing and should be gated out early. Also gives the precise semantics for the 46 ms aim: E1 = first drain whose completion time crosses the second.
findings.test: For every crowded launch in the Sep 21-29 set, pull the block before E1 with full txs: if gasUsed is ~32M or the sum of RLP tx sizes is ~95 KB, the E1 leaders were overflow. Correlate with the fills that missed; if it explains them, add 'previous block near cap' as a no-fire condition and reclaim the wasted shots.

findings.title: eth_sendRawTransactionConditional is live on the Robinhood sequencer host: shots can be dropped at the sequencer for free instead of reverting on-chain
findings.claim: Probing sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com with eth_sendRawTransactionConditional returns 'missing options param', i.e. the method is enabled there. Options: knownAccounts (address -> storage root or slot:value), timestampMin/Max (L2 header time), blockNumberMin/Max (L1 block). The pre-checker validates the options against the latest header and again against a state at least RequiredStateAge=2 s old (walking back at most 4 blocks), and the sequencer's preTxFilter re-checks them at block creation; a failing tx is rejected with -32003 and consumes neither gas nor a nonce. Consequence: timestampMin in the future is rejected at submission (cannot pre-position), but timestampMax = creation+1 drops any shot that would land in E2 or later, and a knownAccounts condition on the curve's reserve slot makes 'first buyer or nothing' free.
findings.relevance: Fees and wasted shots: today the BuyOnce relay handles late or losing shots by reverting on-chain (gas + nonce consumed, and the reverted shot still occupies bytes in the block that count toward the 95 KB cap). A sequencer-side rejection keeps the wallet nonce intact and keeps our own losing shots out of the block.
findings.test: Replay the 35-shot burst on a dry launch with timestampMax set; count rejections vs reverts and confirm no shot lands in E2+. Then run a 50-launch A/B of the 'first-or-nothing' knownAccounts variant against the current second-place-accepting rule using the existing decision-chain backtest.

findings.title: The public feed's delivery order is randomized per message and a second connection arrives first about half the time; third-party feeds measured 16 ms ahead at p50 from us-east-2
findings.claim: nitro's ClientManager.doBroadcast serializes each message once, then iterates the client map (Go map iteration, random order) pushing into each client's channel; per-client writer goroutines then send. The groovg Rust client README reports the public RH feed allows 2 connections per IP (429 on the third), each of two connections is first ~50% of the time, and the duplicate lags ~30 ms on average; permessage-deflate is required. Eira's benchmark (client in AWS us-east-2, 26 Sep 2026): Eira Pulse gRPC first-seen 80.9-88.1%, p50 0.00 ms / p99 0.47 ms lag to first arrival, 16.2 ms median lead over the public feed across 25,597 txs; BlockRazor 'Ultra' p50 0.77 ms and Daris p50 0.52 ms behind Eira. Pricing: Eira day pass $200, Pro $2,000/month; BlockRazor per-day pricing behind login. qskateboard/robinhood-feed-bench is an independent tool that stamps every source on one monotonic clock.
findings.relevance: The two-fleet gate, the 'crowd appears only in the tick's own block' exclusion and the 'created in the last block of its second' exclusion are all bounded by how early the pre-tick blocks are seen; 16 ms is 16% of a block. Using both allowed connections per IP and taking the earliest arrival is free.
findings.test: Run robinhood-feed-bench on the c7a.large for a day with a $200 Eira pass alongside both public-feed connections; then replay the 696 launches with each source's arrival timestamps to count how many additional launches clear the gate one block earlier and what the modelled fills become.

findings.title: Robinhood Chain is pure FCFS today (verified from block data), but Arbitrum One replaced Timeboost with Priority Gas Auctions on 24 Sep 2026 and PGA is a sequencer flag any Arbitrum chain can enable
findings.claim: PGA orders by min(maxPriorityFeePerGas, maxFeePerGas - baseFee) within rounds of B/K (Arbitrum One: 250 ms / 2 = 125 ms rounds; K adjustable 1-10 for two years), ties broken by the sequencer's recorded arrival timestamp, with an anti-starvation boost of p/(2K) per round so zero-fee txs still land within a few blocks; docs state PGA 'is now available for activation across all Arbitrum chains' as a sequencer flag plus a round-count parameter. On Robinhood Chain right now: within the 61 blocks sampled, maxPriorityFeePerGas values are unordered inside blocks (e.g. 757460, 0, 1000000, 1, 0, 21102900) and the RPC reports timeboost_sendExpressLaneTransaction and auctioneer_submitBid as non-existent, so neither Timeboost nor PGA is active.
findings.relevance: Every measured edge (46 ms aim, 2 ms spacing, first-vs-second seat) assumes arrival ordering. If Robinhood flips PGA on, position becomes a priority-fee bid decided per 125 ms-class round and the engine would need a fee-bid mode; conversely, the retirement of Timeboost on Arbitrum One removes the express-lane option as a lever here.
findings.test: Add a daily monitor that checks, per block, whether type-2 txs are sorted by priority fee (PGA signature) and whether new RPC namespaces appear; keep a pre-built fee-bid variant of the shot builder so the switch is a config change.

findings.title: Paid relays claim small but measured wins over the official sequencer host even from Ohio; the same-nonce pair race is the cheap way to verify any path
findings.claim: BlockRazor reports, for its Robinhood 'transaction sending' endpoints (Frankfurt, Ohio, Singapore, Tokyo), a 60.46% win rate over the official sequencer in 703 same-nonce rounds and 54.20% ahead in distinct-nonce runs, measured from three AWS us-east-2 AZs; from Frankfurt/Singapore/Tokyo their relay won 65-70% of 50-pair races. Eira Send (free tier over HTTPS JSON-RPC at send.eiranodes.dev) reports 179/200 = 89.5% success in its own race. Both are vendor benchmarks; the method (two txs, same nonce, different recipient, whichever lands is the winner) is reproducible in minutes.
findings.relevance: Directly targets the 9-point cost of landing second. A 55-60% path advantage from inside Ohio implies the vendors hold better AZ placement or warmer connections than a single c7a.large; the engine can either buy the path or copy the setup (pre-warmed h2 streams from the best AZ).
findings.test: Run 200 same-nonce pairs at random times of day: direct host vs BlockRazor Ohio, direct vs Eira Send, and direct-from-AZ-a vs direct-from-AZ-b/c. Adopt any path that wins >55% with p<0.05, and re-run the live first-place rate (currently ~60%) for a week.

findings.title: Pons v2 snipe tax is a factory-level, owner-mutable formula; the only fee-free E0 path is creator-named exemption
findings.claim: snipeTaxBps(elapsed) = snipeTaxStartBps >> ((elapsed * 14) / snipeTaxSeconds) with factory settings 9900 bps and 3 s gives 99.00% in the launch second, 6.18% at +1 s, 0.19% at +2 s, 0 at +3 s (exactly the E1/E2 numbers measured), applies to buys only, and both parameters are owner-mutable ('read live off the factory'). Exemptions are set at creation by the launching address (launcher, creator-fee recipient, and extra named addresses); currentSnipeTaxBps(recipient) is per-recipient. The open-source bots found (0xhamssog/pons-sniper-bot, Trustdev-eth/pons-sniper-bot-v1-v2) default to waiting until the tax is zero and use a single wallet; neither documents a first-block technique or any measured latency.
findings.relevance: Fees take 36% of gross; this confirms there is no engineering route under 6.18% at E1 other than being named in the creation, and that a silent factory parameter change (e.g. snipeTaxSeconds 3 -> 5, as the docs' '5 seconds' wording hints) would move E1 to ~25% and must be detected before firing.
findings.test: Read snipeTaxStartBps/snipeTaxSeconds from the factory every block in the engine's gate and abort firing on any change; log the value beside each fill.

findings.title: Express-lane research shows auction lanes get captured by three players and 30% of their txs revert; not a path for this venue
findings.claim: The empirical Timeboost study (48.5M express-lane txs, 494k auctions, Jan-Apr 2026) found three entities won 99.74% of rounds, ~30% of express-lane txs reverted, auction revenue declined over time and secondary express-lane markets failed. Timeboost for Arbitrum chains requires the chain owner to deploy ExpressLaneAuction plus an autonomous auctioneer (60 s rounds, 15 s close, 200 ms delay for non-express txs, min reserve 0.001 WETH) and is marked alpha; Robinhood has not deployed it and Arbitrum One has since abandoned it.
findings.relevance: Closes the 'Timeboost express lane' angle: even where it exists the lane is won by capitalized latency shops, and on Robinhood Chain it does not exist. Time is better spent on the FCFS path and on a PGA contingency.
findings.test: None needed beyond the RPC-namespace monitor in the PGA finding.

dead_ends: Timeboost express lane on Robinhood Chain: timeboost_* and auctioneer_* RPC methods absent on both official hosts; Arbitrum One itself retired Timeboost for PGA on 24 Sep 2026.
Arbitrum One's paid Fast Feed (per-tx streaming during block construction, feed-ticket contract): Arbitrum One only, no Robinhood equivalent found.

Nonce-gap pre-positioning (submit nonce N+1 early, trigger with N): nitro's precheckNonces inserts the held tx directly after its predecessor in the same block, so it confers no position; not worth testing.
Oversized gas limit to force retry-queue placement: the gasLimit-based ErrGasLimitReached check only exists for ArbOS < 50; Robinhood runs ArbOS 61 where only gas actually used counts.
timestampMin pre-positioning via conditional transactions: rejected at submission because options are checked against the latest header.
WebSocket submission to the official rpc/sequencer hosts: both return HTTP 400 on upgrade.
YouTube: Ed Felten talks (qxml80TparY, y2jVhQU3cRk) blocked by Google's bot check via fetch; the 'Robinhood Chain sniper bot' videos are marketing with no measurements.
Open-source Pons sniper repos (0xhamssog, Trustdev-eth): single-wallet, wait-until-tax-zero designs, no latency numbers, no first-block method.
0xZetty/arrowhead-protocol: alpha, no data. Glassnode status page: 0 probes online today, only the location statement is usable. cryptotimes 'front-run by two blocks' article: bot wall, unreadable.
Arbitrum research thread 'eth_sendRawTransaction to sequencer?': unanswered.

Chainstack 'What is Robinhood Chain' and Robinhood run-a-full-node page: nitro v3.11.2 and ArbOS 61 only; no sequencer config (max-block-speed, queue sizes) published anywhere; the 100 ms cadence was verified from block timestamps instead.
'Buying Time' (AFT 2023) and 'Shared sequencing as a noisy contest': theory only, no engineering parameters.

findings.title: Pons 'waiver-and-bundle' ring launches have an on-chain signature: 15-25+ SnipeTaxExempted wallets, curve swept 1-3 blocks after creation, insiders hold 82-86% of supply; 467 other clusters run the same play
findings.claim: Wazz (53 launches, $18.43M, Jul 10-Sep 21) and Bitquery (56 launches, $15.5M net; $13.3M buyer losses) reconstructed one crew on Pons V2. Pattern per launch: creator declares 15-25 exempt wallets (up to 31; DEED had 50 wallets funded 16 s before launch, 92 fresh addresses funded ~40 min before), then ONE transaction 1-3 blocks after creation buys for all of them and empties the bonding curve straight into the v4 pool; creator+exempt wallets end with 82-86% of supply (EQUITY: 21 of 31 exempt wallets bought within ~1 s, 65.7%). Only 1.9 ETH of snipe tax was collected across 35 of these launches. Bitquery found 467 further clusters using the same waiver-and-bundle tactic (~$11.6M). 25 of 53 launches used one unverified helper contract deployed Aug 28. Event topics to key on: SnipeTaxExempted 0xe4b7e48f..., SnipeTaxCharged 0x3bc39a55..., CurveBuy 0xec36bf57....
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: fee drag / win rate / 'launches whose crowd appears only in the tick block cannot be taken'. A launch with many exempt wallets is by construction swept before or at E1: our E1 shot either reverts (curve gone), fills on the v4 pool at the insiders' price, or buys into a wall that holds 70-86% of supply and exits in 1-2 swaps. These launches also attract rival fleets, so they may be over-represented in our '2 fleets' gate. Conversely, a cheap pre-tick signal exists: the exempt list is emitted in the creation tx itself.
findings.test: On the 696 qualifying launches join the creation tx's SnipeTaxExempted count (and exempt wallets' share of E0 CurveBuy tokensOut) to the modelled fills; split mean net return and miss rate by exempt-count buckets (0, 1-2, 3-14, 15+). Check how many fills were swept (LaunchSwept/PoolGraduated within 3 blocks of creation). If 15+ exempt launches are net losers or unfillable, add 'exempt_count >= N' as a veto and re-run the backtest.

findings.title: The Pons snipe-tax schedule is owner-mutable and already disagrees across docs (5 s), source (15 s) and chain (3 s): the E1 seat can silently move from 6.18% to 24.75% or 99%
findings.claim: Formula: snipeTaxBps(elapsed) = snipeTaxStartBps >> ((elapsed*14)/snipeTaxSeconds), integer seconds since the launch tx, zero once elapsed >= snipeTaxSeconds. On-chain today: 9900 bps / 3 s => 99% (s0), 6.18% (s1), 0.19% (s2), 0 (s3+). The public docs describe a 5 s decay ('about 25% after one second and 3% after two' = 9900>>2 = 2475 bps, 9900>>5 = 309 bps), and the checked-in factory source defaults to 15 s (which would give 99% at s1, 49.5% at s2, 24.75% at s3). Both constants have setters and events on the factory; creators may exempt up to 32 addresses, fixed at creation. Pons has not (as of Sep 29) announced any change after the Sep 27 exposure, but the parameters are the obvious lever.
findings.relevance: Fee drag (36% of gross) and the whole seat economics: at 5 s the E1 seat costs 24.75%+tier, which turns our +25.4% first-seat gross into a loss; at 15 s no seat before s4 is viable. A silent param change would look exactly like 'P&L hasn't moved' while fills keep landing.
findings.test: Add a watcher on the factory's snipeTax setter events / read snipeTaxStartBps and snipeTaxSeconds (or currentSnipeTaxBps for a shooter address) at every launch, log them with each fill, and compute break-even seat per setting from the backtest's gross-move distribution. Alert and halt firing if the schedule differs from 9900/3.

findings.title: Same-block insider sniping on pump.fun: 87% of snipes profitable, 55% exit within 1 minute, 11% within 15 s, 90% exit in 1-2 swaps, activity 14:00-23:00 UTC (Pine Analytics, 15,000+ launches/month)
findings.claim: Over one month: 15,000+ tokens sniped in the creation block by 4,600+ wallets funded by 10,400+ deployers (~1.75% of launches), 15,000+ SOL realized profit, 87% of snipes profitable, typical 1-100 SOL per wallet. Exit timing: 11%+ fully out within 15 s, 55%+ within 1 min, 85%+ within 5 min; 90%+ of exits use only 1-2 swap events. Activity clusters 14:00-23:00 UTC, near zero 00:00-08:00 UTC ('US-aligned cron jobs').
findings.relevance: (a) Confirms the time-of-day concentration is structural to launchpad sniping, not a quirk of our week (our 75% of money 16-24 UTC). (b) On Pons the analogous insiders are the creator (auto-exempt) and named exempt wallets; their first CurveSell is the insider exit, and it comes in 1-2 swaps inside the first minute, i.e. inside our 11-block hold on many launches.
findings.test: For every fill, record the block of the first CurveSell by the creator/fee-recipient/any exempt wallet relative to our entry block, and the size (share of their holdings). Measure how often it precedes block 11 among losers vs winners. If it separates them, backtest an 'insider-sold' early exit trigger against the fixed 11-block sell (new evidence, distinct from the price/time exit rules already rejected).

findings.title: Independent Pons v2 sniper (bodkin) publishes its full filter set and timing: buys at 0.19% (E2) 1.2-1.6 s after detection, vetoes exempt-wallet bundles, big dev buys, serial deployers with poor graduation history, 'launch-farm fingerprints', missing socials and non-ETH pairs
findings.claim: bodkin subscribes to TokenLaunched, enriches each launch with one aggregate3 multicall + 3 tx reads in ~280 ms, polls currentSnipeTaxBps every 150 ms and buys under a ceiling (measured entries at 0.19% tax, 1.6-2.1 s post-detection; polling entries lagged websocket by 188-203 ms). Vetoes: declared exempt wallets > maxExemptWallets; dev buy > threshold; serial deployers with poor graduation history (in-memory deployer index over 400,000 blocks); launch-farm fingerprint = identical buy amounts + tax from fresh wallets created within 30 min; missing social links; non-ETH pair assets. Exits: TP +80%, SL -35%, trailing 25% off peak, max hold 45 min, marks are live sell quotes net of 1% fee + creator tax + impact. Sep 4 sample: 24,462 launches in 24 h, 559 graduated (2.3%).
findings.relevance: Gate quality and supply. Two signals here were not in the brief's rejected list and are pre-tick computable from the creation tx and the feed: (1) 'fresh-wallet fingerprint' (E0/E1 buyers whose wallets are < 30 min old and share a funder, which matches the Wazz/Bitquery ring pattern of wallets funded 16 s-40 min pre-launch); (2) quote asset (ETH vs USDG/tokenized stock; 33% of Pons launches are stock-quoted per Bitquery).
findings.test: For each qualifying launch compute: share of E0/E1 rival buyers with wallet age < 30 min and a common funding source; quote asset; social links present in metadata. Split modelled fills by each and check whether any explains the 59% win rate or the first-vs-second gap. Also compare bodkin's E2 entry vs our E1 on the same launches using the tax formula (0.19% vs 6.18% seat, one second later).

findings.title: Largest pump.fun predictive study (655,770 tokens): liquidity velocity is the strongest predictor; bot-dominated launches (non-bot share < 30%) have systematically lower sustained inflow; and 92% of tokens with >= 30 swaps get dumped
findings.claim: Sep 1-Oct 1 2025, 655,770 tokens, 0.63% graduated. Conditional on curve level, the number of trades needed to get there dominates every other variable (tokens reaching a level in <= 10 trades vs 50/100/500/1000). Tokens with >= 70% non-bot trades (bot = direct program call, not UI) have higher graduation odds; 'markets dominated by bot-like activity exhibit systematically lower graduation probabilities beyond intermediate stages'. Presence of historically profitable traders: 'at most a modest and non-monotonic effect'. Top-10 serial creators (>= 50 tokens, >= 10 trades/token) beat the economic breakeven only at advanced curve stages, with small n. 92.22% of 184,282 tokens with >= 30 swaps had at least one dump; pre-graduation dumps pay strictly more than post-graduation exits.
findings.relevance: Our gate ('>= 2 rival fleets visible') deliberately selects bot-dominated launches. This paper says such launches have the weakest follow-through beyond the first seconds, which is consistent with our money coming only from the first 11 blocks and with fees eating 36% of gross. Liquidity velocity (few large buys) rather than fleet count may be the better pre-tick proxy for the next-minute move.
findings.test: Recompute the gate using (a) quote inflow per rival shot in the pre-tick blocks and (b) the human (UI / non-relay) share of pre-tick buyers, and compare modelled fills' mean return against the fleet-count gate on the same 696 launches, with the Sep 26-27 low-supply days as a holdout.

findings.title: Rival sniper cohorts raise first-30-minute buyer COUNT by +16.1% but SOL INFLOW by only +6.3% (CI includes zero): crowds bring bodies, not money (1,012 cohorts, 166,098 launches)
findings.claim: Kamat, 1,578,333 buyer events over 166,098 pump.fun launches (Jun 11-25 2026): 1,012 persistent cohorts of 2-12 wallets (2,965 addresses) that co-fire among the first 10 buyers; top cohort (9 wallets) hit 42 launches in 11 days at mean first-buyer rank 2.29; 22 cohorts hit >= 20 launches, median cohort 5. Propensity-matched (5,419 pairs, 10 covariates) effect of cohort presence: first-30-min buyer count +16.1% [+13.0, +19.4]; SOL inflow +6.3% [-0.5, +15.1], not distinguishable from zero; 7.0% of cohort-touched launches had zero non-cohort buyers in 30 min. The paper does not report cohort PnL.
findings.relevance: Direct external evidence on the gate itself: visible fleets predict more transactions but not more quote inflow. Our win (59%) depends on someone paying up after us within 11 blocks; fleet count is a weak proxy for that.
findings.test: Replicate on Pons: cluster rival shooter wallets into persistent cohorts across the 696 launches (co-occurrence >= 3), then regress the 11-block quote inflow (sum of CurveBuy quoteIn from non-cohort wallets) on cohort count vs on pre-tick quote inflow; use whichever predicts inflow to re-rank fireable launches.

findings.title: Sniper landing position elsewhere: 'slot 0 vs slot 2 is a 20-60% upside difference' on pump.fun; co-located sub-35 ms nodes land slot zero 89% vs < 20% at 220 ms; only ~10% of Solana sniper bots are consistently profitable; Robinhood Chain has no Timeboost so ordering is pure arrival time
findings.claim: RPC Fast (240+ events): sub-35 ms detection-to-submission landed slot zero ~89% of events; same logic at 220 ms average latency landed slot zero < 20%; AllenHark: slot 0 vs slot 2 is typically a 20-60% upside gap; Dysnix (Jan 2026): >70% of bots target sub-50 ms but only ~10% deliver consistent profit, attributed to infrastructure not strategy. Chainstack's decoder of the Robinhood feed confirms blockMetadata is always 0 (no express lane): 'ordering is whatever reaches the sequencer first'. Arbitrum FCFS docs: the sequencer appends on arrival; Nitro's bounded queue defaults to 1024 entries and 12 s timeout, after which eth_sendRawTransaction returns 'context deadline exceeded'.
findings.relevance: Our 9-point first-vs-second gap (25.4% vs 16.1%) and 60% first-landing rate are the same shape other venues report, and there is no auction to buy the front seat. The only lever is arrival order at the sequencer ingress under load.
findings.test: From the feed, record for each fill the tx index of our first landed shot vs the first rival shot in the E1 block and the wall-clock send time of both (rival send time inferred from index). Regress win on index gap. Then A/B two ingress paths (direct sequencer endpoint vs RPC gateway, and/or a second AWS AZ) for a week of shadow sends and compare the index distribution; keep whichever lands earlier.

findings.title: Why 400+ rival shots hold the burst for seconds: Nitro seals blocks at a gas target (32 Mgas on Arbitrum One; Orbit default speed limit 7 Mgas/s) and queues the rest FCFS with an exponential basefee ramp; the ArbGasInfo precompile exposes the live gas backlog
findings.claim: Arbitrum One seals a block at the earliest of 32 Mgas target / 95,000 bytes calldata / end of ordering round (64 Mgas effective cap post-Fusaka, 32 Mgas per single tx). Orbit chains default to a 7,000,000 gas/s speed limit (Offchain Labs advises not raising it); when demand exceeds the target the pricer tracks a gas backlog and raises basefee exponentially (~10% fee for 1% over target), and transactions that do not fit simply wait in the FCFS queue. 400 buys at roughly 150-250k gas each is 60-100 Mgas, i.e. 2-3 full blocks at a 32 Mgas cap or ~10 s at 7 Mgas/s. ArbGasInfo.getGasBacklog() and getPricingInertia() are readable precompile views.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck 'under crowds of 400+ rival shots the sequencer holds our burst for seconds and we miss'. If the E1 block is gas-full, no timing trick lands us; but the block-level fullness is observable one block earlier from the feed and the backlog is readable from the precompile, so a crowd-size veto could save the 35-shot gas and the 20% minOut failures.
findings.test: Pull gasUsed/gasLimit for the creation block, E0 blocks and the E1 block of every crowded launch (RPC eth_getBlockByNumber) plus ArbGasInfo.getGasBacklog() at the tick; check whether misses coincide with E1 gasUsed at the cap and a rising backlog. If so, gate on 'projected rival gas in E1 < cap minus our burst' and re-run the miss rate; also confirm Robinhood Chain's actual speed limit and block gas cap (values are chain-owner set).

findings.title: Social-link presence is the strongest cheap pre-launch predictor on pump.fun: Telegram advertised -> 1.485% vs 0.166% graduation (8.94x; Cox HR 5.40), all three socials 1.919% vs 0.110%, on 832,941 launches
findings.claim: Kamat, May 8-Jun 10 2026, 832,941 launches with 24 h outcomes: pooled graduation 0.198% (down 3.18x from 0.63% in Sep-Oct 2025). Telegram link: 1.485% vs 0.166% (log-rank p < 1e-300; multivariate Cox HR 5.40 [4.73, 6.17]); all three channels 1.919% vs none 0.110%; Cox concordance 0.858 with only creation-time fields (socials, initial mcap, description length). Dataset (860,213 rows) is public on Zenodo.
findings.relevance: Supply and win rate: a creation-time field that separates launches by ~9x in follow-through elsewhere and that bodkin also uses as a veto on Pons. It is available before the tick from the launch metadata and costs nothing in latency.
findings.test: Parse socials/description length from Pons launch metadata (URI or creation calldata) for the 696 launches; split modelled fills and misses by 'any social' / 'Telegram' / 'none'; if the lift transfers, use it as a tie-breaker to fire on more single-fleet launches on low-supply days rather than as a veto.

findings.title: Copycat launches graduate 0.86% vs 9.20% for originals; top 1% of creator clusters make 58.57% of all coins; wash-traded coins graduate 2.0% vs 0.90% (15.2M pump.fun coins)
findings.claim: Two years of pump.fun (Jan 2024-Jan 2026, 15.2M coins, 5.8M creator addresses). After 3-hop address clustering, the top 1% of clusters created 58.57% of coins (largest cluster 10,531 addresses; top 100 clusters active 434 days on average). 1.49M copycat coins (10%): copycats graduate 0.86% vs 9.20% for the originals they copy; 26.5% of copycats are created outside the UI. Coins with detectable wash trading graduate 2.0% vs 0.90%; with 500+ wash trades 9.64%. 4,402 atomic multi-sender dumps found (median 7 senders, max 312).
findings.relevance: Selection: name/symbol duplication of a recently trending launch is a pre-tick, zero-latency feature not in the brief's list (creator serial count was). Wash/atomic-bundle activity being positively associated with graduation is also consistent with our crowd gate working at all.
findings.test: Flag each qualifying launch whose name or symbol matches a launch created in the prior 24 h that reached >= X quote inflow (or any hood.fun/Pons trending list); compare modelled net return and miss rate for copycats vs originals; test whether firing only on the 'original' of a copy wave changes the Sep 26-27 supply.

findings.title: Pons-wide numbers (Bitquery, Aug 3-Sep 3 2026): 1.55% graduate, median 4 min to graduation, 83.6% of graduations within 1 h, 66.8% of 314,736 wallets lost, and the ~1,000 high-frequency wallets (>25% of volume) are 'deep in the red'
findings.claim: 207,893 coins in the window, 3,228 graduated (1.55%); median graduation 4 min, 83.6% inside one hour, fastest in the creation block (PDEX, 10 s). Daily launches went from ~2,000 (early Aug) to ~20,000 (late Aug), curve trading rose ~55x in 11 days. $736M traded on curves vs $2.14B on v4 pools. 314,736 wallets: 66.8% lost (median loss ~$5); winners took $33.9M, losers gave up $77.3M. About 1,000 wallets with 1,000+ trades each were over 25% of volume and net negative; nine wallets showed near-identical patterns across thousands of coins. Quote assets: ETH $406M (113,181 coins), stables $98.5M (20,440), tokenized stocks $232M (73,896 coins, NVDA first). Fees ~1% per side, ~80% to creators; only 16 creators cleared $10k.
findings.relevance: Regime and supply: the rival fleets we gate on are, in aggregate, losing money on Pons, and launch count is the dominant driver of fireable supply (our 20-33 -> 6-11 fills/day). Tokenized-stock-quoted launches are a third of supply and were never split out in our backtest.
findings.test: Split the 696 launches and modelled fills by quote asset (ETH / USDG / stock) and by day-level launch count; check whether stock-quoted launches carry the same fee structure and crowd and whether they are a separate, less-contested pool of fireable launches on low-supply days.

findings.title: Other launchpads' anti-snipe economics, and a zero-snipe-tax venue on the same chain: four.meme X Mode 100% -> 1% by block 6, Zora 99% -> 1% over 10 s, Clanker ~80% -> 5% over ~30 s plus a gas-bid sniper auction every 2 blocks; hood.fun on Robinhood Chain charges a flat 1% with no snipe tax but a 5%-of-curve per-wallet cap
findings.claim: four.meme X Mode (Oct 30 2025): fee 100% at block 0 decreasing block by block to the 1% normal rate at block 6. Zora: 99% in the first second decaying to 1% over ten seconds. Clanker v4: launch fee ~80% decaying to ~5% over ~30 s, and ClankerSniperAuctionV0: up to 5 auctions, one every 2 blocks, snipers bid by gas price above a peg and pay (gasPrice - peg) x paymentPerGasUnit in WETH, 80/20 to token rewards/factory. hood.fun (Robinhood Chain): 1% flat curve fee (80% to creator), no snipe tax; optional launch-window per-wallet cap and a 5%-of-curve per-wallet cap on by default; 80% of supply on curve, ~6.5 ETH to graduate; migration fee 0.05 ETH + 3% of raise + 0.5 ETH. Pools.trade uses a 4-hour TWAP auction. Pons: 1% curve fee, creator tax fixed at creation, 4.2 ETH graduation (ETH pairs).
findings.relevance: Fee drag: our 8.9% average seat cost is 36% of gross. On hood.fun the same sequencer-feed engine could fire in the creation block (E0) for 1% + impact, with the 5% per-wallet cap bounding stake per shooter (35 shooters already exist). Unknowns are hood.fun's launch count and crowd size.
findings.test: Count hood.fun factory launches/day from the feed for the same Sep 21-29 week, measure E0/E1 rival shots per launch and the 11-block price path, then re-run the identical rule with a 1% fee and E0 entry; compare fills/day and mean net to Pons. Verify the per-wallet cap and whether creation-block buys are permitted by reading the curve contract.

findings.title: Only public sniper backtest with fee-aware numbers: 270 exit setups on 2,551,714 pump.fun events found dev-buy >= 1 SOL, +30% TP / -30% SL / 120 s max hold: 1,034 trades, 52.7% win, +40.26 SOL in one hour; round-trip break-even 2.55%; 20% slippage needed live
findings.claim: Author replayed one hour (2,042 new tokens, 1,036 with dev buys >= 1 SOL) through the real curve math and swept dev-buy thresholds {1,3,5,10,20 SOL} x targets 5-200% x stops {15,30,50%} x max holds {120,300,900 s}. Best: entry on dev buy >= 1 SOL, TP +30%, SL -30%, 120 s => 1,034 trades, 52.7% win, +40.26 SOL. Break-even move 2.55% (1.25% fee each side). Live needs ~20% slippage because the pool moves between decision and confirmation. Claims ~$4,000/day on good days, far less on quiet days.
findings.relevance: Selection: the creator's own opening buy size (creator is auto-exempt on Pons, so its buy lands in the creation block and is visible before the tick) as a continuous gate feature; also independent confirmation that ~20% slippage and a 2-minute horizon are where fee-aware snipes cluster.
findings.test: For each of the 696 launches compute the creator/fee-recipient CurveBuy quoteIn in the creation second (USD), bucket into quartiles, and compare modelled net return and win rate per bucket; if monotonic, add it to the gate as a tie-breaker on single-fleet launches to recover supply on low days.

dead_ends: No published study quantifies return by buyer rank (1st vs 2nd vs 3rd) on any bonding-curve venue; the only numbers are vendor claims (AllenHark '20-60% slot 0 vs slot 2'). The Kamat cohort paper records buyer rank but reports no PnL.
YouTube: every hit for pump.fun / Robinhood Chain sniper bots is a tutorial or bot advertisement ('10000% ROI'); Google blocked fetching video pages, and no video with measured data was found.

findings.title: Sequencer endpoint accepts eth_sendRawTransactionConditional with an L2 timestampMin/timestampMax window: let the sequencer reject any shot that would land in the creation second, instead of aiming 46 ms early
findings.claim: Arbitrum Nitro sequencer endpoints accept only eth_sendRawTransaction and eth_sendRawTransactionConditional. The conditional form carries knownAccounts (address -> storage root or slot=value), blockNumberMin/Max (L1 block numbers) and timestampMin/timestampMax (L2 timestamp). The sequencer verifies the conditions before accepting; if any fails the tx is rejected with JSON-RPC error -32003 and is never included (no gas burned, nonce not consumed). Robinhood Chain runs stock Nitro (chain 4663, no Timeboost), so the same method should be exposed at sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com.
findings.relevance: Bottlenecks: E1 aim (46 ms before the boundary), 'launches created in the last block of their second cannot be aimed at', wasted shots when the sequencer holds the burst. Since the Pons tax is keyed on block.timestamp second, a shot sent with timestampMin = creationTs+1 and timestampMax = creationTs+1 can only ever execute at E1; anything the sequencer would place in the creation second (97% tax) or in E2+ is rejected for free. If Nitro evaluates the condition against the block being built (preTxFilter at sequencing time), a spray of conditional shots starting ~100 ms before the boundary gets the first accepted shot into the first block of the new second with the sequencer's own clock, which also makes last-block-of-second creations aimable. If instead it evaluates on arrival, it still converts 97%-tax fills and minOut reverts into zero-cost rejections and gives an exact 'too early' signal per shot for calibrating the 46 ms lead.
findings.test: 1) From the c7a.large, send a dust self-transfer via eth_sendRawTransactionConditional to sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com with timestampMin = now+1 s: record whether the reply is an immediate -32003, a hold until the timestamp, or a method-not-found. 2) If accepted, replay 20 live launches with half the 35 shooters conditional (min=max=creationTs+1) and half unconditional; compare landed-second distribution, gas burned, and first-vs-second place. 3) Check whether repeated rejections trigger sequencer rate limiting (count 429s).

findings.title: BlockRazor's Ohio A/B: private ingress beat the official sequencer endpoint 60.46% of same-nonce races from us-east-2; the public feed trails their feed by 28-953 ms depending on Ohio AZ
findings.claim: BlockRazor (vendor, self-interested) reports: from Ohio, their submission path won 60.46% of same-nonce races and was ahead in 54.62% of distinct-nonce tests against https://sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com; from Frankfurt/Singapore/Tokyo 70%/65%/65% over 50 nonce-identical pairs per region. Feed lag measured over 13,251 blocks on 10 Sep 2026: official wss://feed.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com arrived 28-85 ms (use2-az1), 97-953 ms (use2-az2) and 27-111 ms (use2-az3) after BlockRazor's feed, which reported 0 ms P50-P99. Their node-required 'Ultra' feed costs $200/day or $2,000/month; endpoints wss://us.robinhood-feeder.blockrazor.io/ws/ultra/{token} (Ohio) and jp.* (Tokyo). Glassnode's latency page confirms the sequencer is on AWS us-east-2 and that ordering is strictly first-come-first-served with no fee priority (the page currently shows 0/0 probes online).
findings.relevance: Bottlenecks: landing second instead of first (9 points), and the E1 boundary estimate. If our engine derives the boundary from the public feed's arrival time, a 28-111 ms (one block) feed lag in az1/az3, or up to 953 ms in az2, biases the aim by up to a full block; and a 60/40 same-nonce edge from the same region would directly move the 60% first-place rate.
findings.test: Replicate their protocol from our box: 100 pairs of identical-nonce dust txs, one to sequencer.mainnet, one to a BlockRazor or bloXroute Ohio endpoint, count which lands; separately, log feed message arrival time vs the block's own timestamp across 1,000 blocks and check which Ohio AZ the instance is in (use2-az2 is the bad one). Adopt only if the same-nonce win rate exceeds 55% and the feed lag reduction is at least one block.

findings.title: Identical-nonce multi-path spraying: send each shooter's signed tx through two ingress paths at once; the first to reach the sequencer wins, the duplicate is a free nonce rejection
findings.claim: BlockRazor's own benchmark is built on this: 'pairs of transactions with identical nonces' sent to two endpoints, only one can be sequenced, the loser is rejected as a nonce conflict at no cost. Under FCFS with no fee priority, path diversity is the only cheap way to buy arrival-time variance. Twelve public HTTPS ingress points exist for chain 4663 (Robinhood, bloXroute robinhood.rpc.blxrbdn.com, dRPC, Tenderly, Allnodes, etc.) plus the sequencer endpoint; Banana Gun cites an 88% first-block rate on Ethereum from bundle infrastructure with multi-wallet distribution but gives no Robinhood numbers.
findings.relevance: Bottlenecks: first vs second place, and the multi-second holds under 400+ rival shots (a second path may not be queued behind the same backlog). Cost is only bandwidth: rejected duplicates burn no gas.
findings.test: For 30 launches, send each of the 35 shots simultaneously to sequencer.mainnet and to one alternate ingress (bloXroute public or BlockRazor Ohio); tag each copy and read back which copy's hash landed; measure change in landed-first share and in reply latency under crowds; verify the sequencer does not penalise the duplicate stream (429 count).

findings.title: Pons V2 tax internals confirmed on-chain and now productised: 9900 >> ((elapsed*14)/3) bps, keyed on recipient, exemptions max 32 fixed at creation; PumpDev's public API ships 'maxSnipeTaxBps: 700' as the E1 setting
findings.claim: Casatrick (18 Sep 2026) gives the deployed formula snipeTaxBps(elapsed) = snipeTaxStartBps >> ((elapsed*14)/snipeTaxSeconds) with factory values 9900/3, i.e. 99.00%, 6.18%, 0.19%, 0 — matching the brief's E1/E2. Official docs say the tax lasts 5 s and the published source says 15 s; the realorrug capture (launch block 62357124) confirms the chain runs 3 s, so 'Pons's published source does not match what is deployed'. Tax is keyed on the token recipient, readable per-address via curve.currentSnipeTaxBps(recipient); the launch call carries snipeTaxExemptions[] (selector 0xa72101af), max 32 entries or revert ExemptionListTooLong, creator and fee recipient auto-exempt, immutable after creation, and a launch tx may carry an exempt buy. PumpDev's hosted API documents maxSnipeTaxBps: 700 as 'takes the second second (6.18%)', 20 for the third, HTTP 425 with retry timing otherwise, default priority fee 0.05 gwei, base fee ~0.2 gwei, tips seen 0.02-1.5 gwei, recommended slippage 15-25%.
findings.relevance: Bottlenecks: supply of fireable launches falling (20-33/day to 6-11/day) and crowding at E1. E1 is now a one-parameter setting in a commercial API, so the rival population at E1 can grow without any engineering; and the factory parameters demonstrably differ from documentation and can change, which would silently move the seat the engine aims at.
findings.test: (a) For each of the 696 launches, count distinct E1 buyers and classify by tx shape (PumpDev-routed calldata vs direct curve calls) week over week to see if E1 crowd growth explains the supply drop. (b) Read snipeTaxStartBps and snipeTaxSeconds from factory 0x7eD598BcEf8bd9Edd8C97A195C6d13f40801EC7e on every launch and alarm on change. (c) Verify the relay's fill check uses the CurveBuy(buyer, recipient, quoteIn, tokensOut, fee, tax) event's tax field, not tx status.

findings.title: Exempt-wallet bundle ring: 53-56 launches, $15.5-18.4M, 15-25 exempt wallets buying 70-86% of supply in one tx 1-3 blocks after creation via one bundler contract deployed 28 Aug; 467 other clusters use the same tactic
findings.claim: Wazz (pseudonymous analyst, thread paywalled) and Bitquery independently trace a crew: 53 launches 10 Jul-21 Sep ($18.43M) / 56 launches to 23 Sep ($15.5M, $12.4M strict). Pattern: creator names 15-25 snipeTaxExemptions; one transaction 1-3 blocks after creation buys for all of them, empties the curve and pushes straight to the v4 pool, leaving creator+exempt wallets 82-86% of supply 'in under a second'; 25 of the 53 launches used one unverified bundling contract created 28 Aug ('a commercial bundling tool with many unrelated users'); for DEED, one wallet funded 92 fresh addresses ~40 min before launch and 25 exempt wallets took ~two-thirds of supply. Snipe tax collected by Pons across 35 of these launches: 1.9 ETH. Bitquery counts 467 other clusters using the same tactic for a potential $11.6M. Top extractions CRUMBS $3.12M, LEGS $2.9M, PINK $1.44M.
findings.relevance: Bottlenecks: 'launches whose crowd appears only in the tick's own block cannot be taken' and the supply drop. Exempt-bundle launches graduate inside the creation second, so they are structurally unfireable, and a growing share of the hottest-looking launches (many named buyers, big creation-block volume) are of this type; the engine already reads the exemption list, so exempt-list length and the bundler contract address are free pre-tick features.
findings.test: Join the 696-launch backtest with exemption-list length, whether the creation tx routed through the 28-Aug bundler contract, and whether the curve graduated before E1; measure what share of the 'crowd present' launches this removes and whether any of the 130 modelled fills sit on such launches. If the two-fleet gate is counting exempt wallets' buys as rival fleets, add 'exemptions >= 10 -> skip' and re-run.

findings.title: Pools.trade (Uniswap Labs' launchpad on Robinhood Chain, live 5 Aug 2026): Instant Launch is a bonding curve with no snipe tax and a 0.25% LP fee, 'thousands of launches per day at peak'
findings.claim: Instant Launch: classic bonding curve, no FDV requirement, liquidity permanently locked in a v4 pool, 1B fixed supply, native ETH quote, pool fee 2500 (0.25%), no hook (0x000...000), tick spacing 25, creator may take 0.05% of the 25 bps; no launchpad fee; the only anti-snipe measure is that the creator buys in the same block as creation. Crowd Launch is a 4-hour TWAP auction with a $10K FDV threshold. Contracts: launch entry 0x0000ffffbe8efe702c8703ae3477ff5de3d319c0 (current), token factory 0x000000e200088d55c39a11f609e5f667729ad49b, v4 PoolManager 0x8366a39cc670b4001a1121b8f6a443a643e40951; launches emit TokenCreated(token). Casatrick describes it as 'a pure speed game rather than a tax-timing game'.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: fees take 36% of gross (8.9% avg on Pons) — the same relay, fleet and feed could fire on a venue where the round trip costs ~0.5% plus curve impact. The trade-off is that with no tax the entire crowd targets the creation block, so the 'two fleets before the tick' gate has no tick to observe; the gate would have to be rebuilt on creation-tx features.
findings.test: Replay Pools.trade TokenCreated events for 21-29 Sep from the feed: count creation-block and block+1 buyers per launch, price path over the next 11 blocks, and simulate the $13 stake with 0.25% fee and curve impact at first/second/third position. Compare fills per day and net per fill against the 130 Pons fills.

findings.title: Ingress and queue facts behind the multi-second holds: public RPC 429s after ~6 quick calls, sequencer endpoint is sendRaw-only, Nitro queue 1024/12 s, blocks slow under load (2% fewer blocks on the 3 Sep congestion day), feed rate-limited per client
findings.claim: Dwellir (23 Sep 2026): rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com 'returned HTTP 429 after about six quick calls', keeps ~10 min of state, is documented as 'not for production'. Nitro sequencer defaults: queue-size 1024, queue-timeout 12 s, max-block-speed 250 ms (Robinhood runs 100 ms), max-tx-data-size 95000. Bitquery: on 3 Sep the chain produced 842,360 blocks vs 861,465 on a calm day (2% fewer) while gas used tripled; base fee went 0.02 -> 0.511 gwei in 11 days; eight addresses drove four-fifths of demand. Chainstack: feed rate limiting is per client not per connection; one message = one block, sequence number = L2 block number; a single block carried 85 txs; ArbOS 61 compliance filtering can void a tx after sequencing (status 0x0, no logs, gas burned; ~150 filtered txs/day, filterer 0xebDc18A1...24b7 with 6,092 txs by mid-Aug); a sequencer failover can reorder before the batch lands.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: 'under crowds of 400+ rival shots the sequencer holds our burst for seconds'. If any shooter's tx goes to rpc.mainnet rather than sequencer.mainnet, the burst is serialised by a 6-call rate limit; and with block cadence stretching under load, the E1 block may arrive late relative to wall-clock, so a fixed 46 ms lead lands early. Also: BuyOnce's 'first shot that lands' must not treat a voided status-0 inclusion as a fill.
findings.test: From the engine's logs, per shot: endpoint used, HTTP status, reply latency, landed block number; correlate reply latency with rival-shot count and with inter-block spacing from feed sequence numbers over the same second; scan past shot receipts for status 0 with empty revert data. If holds coincide with stretched block spacing, the sequencer is the bottleneck; if they coincide with 429s, it is ingress.

findings.title: Pine Analytics (Solana, Apr 2025): deployer-funded same-block snipers cluster 14:00-23:00 UTC, 87% of snipes profitable, 15,000 SOL/month, 55% fully out within 60 s and 11% within 15 s
findings.claim: Over one month on pump.fun: 15,000+ tokens sniped in the launch block by wallets funded directly by the deployer, 4,600+ sniper wallets, 10,400+ deployers, ~1.75% of launches, 15,000 SOL realised, 87% of snipes profitable, per-wallet profit typically 1-100 SOL. Exits: 11% within 15 s, 55% within 60 s, 85% within 5 min, >90% of exits in one or two swaps. Activity clustered 14:00-23:00 UTC with hub-and-spoke funding (one deployer funding dozens of wallets) and single-use burners.

The same UTC window shows up for the professional insider cohort on Solana, which suggests the concentration is structural (US-hours operators and their audiences) rather than a one-week artifact, and that insider selling begins within 15 s for a meaningful minority — inside or just after our 11-block hold. The funding-pattern heuristic (fresh wallets funded minutes before the launch by the creator's funder) is a pre-tick feature we can compute from the feed.
