findings.title: Nitro block composition is a ~10 ms read window per 100 ms block: 'first in E1' is decided ~80-90 ms before E1 is built (verified in sequencer.go)
findings.claim: In Nitro's createBlock (execution/gethexec/sequencer.go, master): each block's batch is built by (1) draining txRetryQueue first (leftovers from the previous block that did not fit, in FIFO order), then (2) blocking until the first txQueue item arrives, then pulling further items for only ReadFromTxQueueTimeout (default 10 ms) once >=2 items are in hand, then executing. The next createBlock starts MaxBlockSpeed after the previous one started (100 ms on Robinhood). The block timestamp is time.Now().Unix() taken after the read window. On chain 4663 ArbGasInfo.getGasAccountingParams() returns speedLimit 7,000,000 gas/s, perBlockGasLimit 32,000,000, maxTxGas 32,000,000 (header gasLimit is the dummy 2^50). Txs beyond 32M gas are pushed to txRetryQueue in order and lead the next block; the tx queue is a 1024-slot channel with a 12 s queue timeout. Consequence: the first position in block k+1 goes to the earliest arrival after block k's read window closed, i.e. a window of roughly 90 ms that opens about 10 ms after block k's first tx and closes when block k+1 is built; position inside it is pure arrival order.
findings.relevance: Landing second instead of first costs 9 points (+25.4% vs +16.1%) and live we land first only ~60%. The current burst (fire 46 ms before the E1 boundary, 2 ms spacing over 35 shots = 70 ms span) is calibrated empirically; this model says the front of E1 is decided by arrivals in the first 10-20 ms after block E1-1's window closes, so shots in the tail of the 70 ms span cannot be first, and the burst should be front-loaded earlier with the timestamp guard living in the BuyOnce contract (require block.timestamp >= E1 second) rather than in the send schedule.
findings.test: From the engine's fill log, regress our tx index-in-block on send offset relative to the E1 boundary and locate the offset at which index-in-block jumps from 0 to >0 (that is the previous block's window edge). Then A/B on live launches: burst centred at -46 ms vs -70 ms and -85 ms, with the on-chain guard; compare first-place rate. Also confirm Robinhood did not override read-from-tx-queue-timeout by sending two txs 15 ms apart from two wallets and checking whether they split across blocks.
findings.confidence: high on the mechanics (read from source), medium on the tuning gain (Robinhood's flag values are not public)

findings.title: Under a 400-shot crowd the L2 base fee ramps (speed limit 7M gas/s) and Nitro drops txs whose maxFeePerGas < baseFee instead of delaying them
findings.claim: Robinhood Chain's ArbOS speed limit is 7,000,000 gas/s with 32,000,000 gas per block (read from the ArbGasInfo precompile 0x6C on chain 4663); current base fee is 20,156,000 wei (0.02 gwei). A 400-shot crowd at ~250-400k gas per bonding-curve buy is 100-160M gas inside about one second, 15-20x the speed limit, which is exactly what ArbOS's backlog-based pricing responds to by raising the base fee over the next blocks. In createBlock, any queued tx with GasFeeCap < lastBlock.BaseFee is returned immediately with core.ErrFeeCapTooLow ('max fee per gas less than block base fee') and never retried. Separately, MaxRevertGasReject defaults to 0, so every reverted shot (minOut guard, BuyOnce losers if they revert) is included and pays gas. The pre-checker also rejects a tx when balance < value + gasLimit*maxFeePerGas, so a high fee cap must be covered by the shooter wallet's balance.
findings.relevance: Touches the 'under crowds of 400+ rival shots the sequencer holds our burst for seconds and we miss' bottleneck: part of those misses may be silent fee-cap rejections rather than queueing, and the fix is free on an FCFS chain (you pay only the base fee, the cap is not a bid).
findings.test: Pull the engine's RPC error strings for the crowd events (look for 'max fee per gas less than block base fee' and 'context deadline exceeded'); from the feed, reconstruct the per-block base fee path in the 2 s after each crowded launch; then set maxFeePerGas to >= 50x the quiet base fee (e.g. 1-2 gwei) and confirm each shooter wallet holds gasLimit*maxFee + stake. Re-measure miss rate under crowds.
findings.confidence: medium (fee dynamics are ArbOS-standard; whether the engine's current cap is too low is unknown)

findings.title: Duplicate the same signed shot over several ingress paths to the one sequencer; the loser copy is free. BlockRazor measured 60.46% same-nonce wins vs the official sequencer endpoint from Ohio
findings.claim: Solana snipers fan one signed tx out to every provider simultaneously: D3AD-E/Solana-sniper-bot (Rust, 4 stars, last commit 2026-09-14) writes the same durable-nonce tx to 11 provider sockets (Jito, Helius, bloXroute, Nozomi, Blockrazor, Falcon, Flashblock, Nextblock, Node1, Astralane, 0slot) with per-thread tip stamping in <1 ms; girasolbot (Rust, 0 stars) aborts the losing provider tasks after the first success. On Robinhood there is one sequencer but several ingress paths: the official sequencer endpoint https://sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com (documented by Robinhood; accepts eth_sendRawTransaction and eth_sendRawTransactionConditional), the public RPC, Alchemy/Chainstack/QuickNode forwarders, and BlockRazor's Robinhood send endpoints (Frankfurt, Ohio, Singapore, Tokyo). Duplicates cost nothing: Nitro's precheckNonces keeps the second same-nonce copy 'in case previous txs fail', it then fails its nonce check at execution and is not included. BlockRazor's own benchmark (703 rounds, Ohio, same nonce raced against the official sequencer endpoint): 60.46% wins for their route, 54.20% 'same block, earlier index', 0.43% earlier block; from Frankfurt/Singapore/Tokyo 65-70% vs 30-35%. Pricing for the send product is not published ('contact sales').
findings.relevance: Directly targets first-vs-second (9 points) and the 60% first-place rate: 'same block, earlier index' is exactly the quantity we lose on. Also insures against one path stalling during 400-shot crowds.
findings.test: Replicate BlockRazor's methodology from our c7a.large: for 500+ rounds send one signed tx (fresh nonce) simultaneously to the official sequencer endpoint, the public RPC and Alchemy WS, and record which path's copy is included and its index; then trial BlockRazor's send endpoint the same way for a day before paying. Adopt fan-out to the best two paths for every shot.
findings.confidence: high that duplicates are free (code), medium on the vendor's numbers

findings.title: Feed timing: open both allowed sockets per IP (second copy is ~30 ms late on average), pick the right us-east-2 AZ (native feed P99 up to 953 ms in use2-az2), or rent the $200/day ultra feed
findings.claim: groovg/ultrafast-robinhood-sequencer-feed (Rust, 5 stars, last commit 2026-09-28) measured against wss://feed.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com: 'The public feed allows two connections per IP, and a third gets HTTP 429'; with two sockets 'each got about half the messages first. The other copy showed up about 30 ms later on average, sometimes 100 ms later'; busy-polling cut socket-read-to-recv from 95 to 61 us; sender recovery costs 273 us/message; signature check 27 us. chainstacklabs/robinhood-chain-sequencer-feed (Python, 30 stars, last commit 2026-09-25, pins nitro v3.12.0-ebe9e83 'the build mainnet runs') decodes lazily (4 us basic fields, 10 us hash, 70 us sender) but warns the Nitro relay 'doesn't check signatures, and it hides reorgs because it drops any message whose sequence number it has already sent'. BlockRazor's benchmark of Robinhood's native feed vs their node-required Ultra feed across the three Ohio AZs: native feed P50 27-97 ms behind, use2-az2 P99 953 ms; Tokyo native P50 71 ms; Ultra feed is WebSocket into a local node, $200/unit/day or $2,000/month, Ohio and Tokyo endpoints. Robinhood also documents a delayed backup feed wss://delayed-feed.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com running ~500 ms behind.
findings.relevance: The E1 tick estimate and the creation detection both come from the feed; tens of ms of feed jitter is the same order as the 46 ms pre-aim, so it feeds straight into first-vs-second and into 'launches created in the last block of their second cannot be aimed at'. AZ placement is a one-time fix on the existing AWS setup.
findings.test: Run two feed sockets plus the delayed feed for 24 h and log per-block arrival deltas (median and P99 of second-minus-first). Launch a t3.micro in each other us-east-2 AZ running the same logger for a day and compare per-AZ arrival times against the sequencer endpoint's RTT; move the engine if an AZ is consistently earlier. Only then trial the Ultra feed for one day against the two-socket baseline.
findings.confidence: medium-high (independent measurements by two parties, but AZ numbers are vendor-published)

findings.title: eth_sendRawTransactionConditional on the sequencer endpoint gives 'first-or-nothing' shots and wrong-second rejections at zero gas (verified in Nitro pre-checker and preTxFilter)
findings.claim: Nitro sequencer endpoints accept eth_sendRawTransactionConditional with options knownAccounts (address -> storage root or slot->value map), timestampMin/Max (L2 block time, seconds) and blockNumberMin/Max (note: L1 block number, not L2). The tx pre-checker (defaults: strictness 20 'LikelyCompatible', required-state-age 2 s, required-state-max-blocks 4) checks the options against the head state and against the state up to 4 blocks back (400 ms at 100 ms blocks, the block cap binds before the 2 s age); the sequencer re-checks in preTxFilter against the in-block state at the tx's position; any failure returns JSON-RPC -32003 and the tx is never included, so no gas is paid (unlike today's reverted shots, which are included because max-revert-gas-reject defaults to 0). A shot with knownAccounts = {curve: {tokensSold slot: initial value}} therefore executes only if no buy precedes it in the block and the chain, i.e. a 'first-or-nothing' shot; timestampMin = E1 second turns a shot that arrives in the creation second into a free rejection instead of a 20%-slippage revert.
findings.relevance: Two bottlenecks: (a) capacity/stake ($13 because untested above): put larger stake only on shots that can only fill first (+25.4% mean) and keep normal small shots behind them, BuyOnce still buys once; (b) shots that land in the wrong second cost gas today. Caveat: the 4-blocks-back check means the expected slot value must also hold 400 ms earlier, so either pick a slot whose pre-creation value (0) equals its no-buys value, or only use it when the creation sits in the first half of its second.
findings.test: Send a conditional tx to https://sequencer.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com with a deliberately false knownAccounts value and confirm -32003 with no on-chain trace, then with a true value and confirm inclusion; check Robinhood has not set required-state-age higher by testing a slot that changed 600 ms ago. Then shadow-run a two-tier burst (5 first-only shots at $40 ahead of 30 normal $13 shots) on the 130-fill backtest using the recorded index-in-block to score which tier would have filled.
findings.confidence: medium (code verified on master; Robinhood's pre-checker flags and Pons curve slot layout unverified)

findings.title: Regime risk: Arbitrum One moved from FCFS to Priority Gas Auctions on 2026-09-24 and Robinhood already runs a nitro v3.12.0 build; a daily canary should detect the switch
findings.claim: Arbitrum One launched PGA on 2026-09-24: intake goes to an unordered waiting list, and at the start of every round (block time B / K rounds; 125 ms on Arbitrum One) the list is moved into a priority queue keyed on priority_fee_per_gas = min(maxPriorityFee, maxFee - baseFee), ties broken by sequencer arrival timestamp; Arbitrum docs say PGA is 'now available for activation across all Arbitrum chains'. The companion paid Fast Feed streams ordering during block construction. Robinhood's docs pin nitro v3.11.2 for full nodes, but Chainstack's relay PR #11 (2026-09-25) pins 'nitro v3.12.0-ebe9e83, the build mainnet runs', newer than the latest public nitro release v3.11.4 (2026-09-16), i.e. a PGA-era build. Robinhood docs and Chainstack (2026-09-25) still describe strict FCFS with no Timeboost, and Timeboost's own record (arXiv 2509.22143: 30.49% of express-lane txs reverted, three entities won 99.74% of auctions) shows how fast an auction regime concentrates the seat.
findings.relevance: Every measured edge (46 ms aim, first-vs-second split, burst spacing) is an FCFS artifact. If Robinhood enables PGA, first-in-block becomes a fee bid decided every 125 ms and the Solana-style dynamic tip logic (RPC Fast: tip floor multiplied 10-50x within seconds around hot launches) becomes the transferable technique instead.
findings.test: Daily canary: from two wallets in the same block window send tx A (priority fee 0) and 30 ms later tx B (priority fee 1 gwei); under FCFS A always precedes B, under PGA B precedes A whenever both fall in one round. Also diff the block ordering in the feed against tx maxPriorityFeePerGas for a few busy blocks each day and alert on any monotone fee ordering.
findings.confidence: high on the facts, low-medium on the probability that Robinhood flips it

findings.title: Copy the Solana bots' measurement discipline: multi-lane detection races run in separate processes, and per-fill 'blocks after creation + index in block' percentiles
findings.claim: chainstacklabs/pumpfun-bonkfun-bot (Python, ~1.0k stars, last commit 2026-09-28) ships compare_listeners.py racing five lanes (geyser, logs, blocks, shreds, pumpportal); a published run: shreds first on 16/19 coins (84.2%), geyser +29.1 ms, logs +104.7 ms, blocks +291.7 ms behind shreds. Issue #213/PR #230 found that running the gRPC and websocket lanes in one asyncio event loop starved the websocket lane (16,577 of 71,568 frames received, 27 of 117 coins reported) and fixed it by giving each lane its own process. Its buy path also has a 'zero-RPC' mode (trust the CreateEvent, no curve read) and a 2.0 s curve_refresh_budget. Tinuz/solsniperbot (TypeScript, 0 stars, last commit 2026-09-27) dashboards 'landed slots after launch' percentiles, detect->send latency, and reads its own fill from the same stream at 'processed'. D3AD-E reconciles orphan positions every 60 s with a force-sell.
findings.relevance: A Python 3.11 engine that decodes the feed, signs 35 shots and issues 35 sends on one asyncio loop is exposed to the same starvation during bursts, which would show up as late tick detection exactly when it matters; and the engine's key numbers (first-place rate, blocks-after-creation, index-in-block per fill) are the analog of the slot-delta dashboards. Orphan reconciliation matters with 35 shooter wallets and 4 s sequencer replies.
findings.test: Instrument feed-message handling latency (recv timestamp minus message timestamp) during bursts with the feed reader in-process vs in a separate process via multiprocessing/shared memory; move it out if P99 grows during bursts. Add a lane race (feed socket 1, feed socket 2, delayed feed, Alchemy newHeads) logging first-detection per launch. Add a 60 s reconciler that scans the 35 wallets for unexpected token balances.

findings.title: Public Pons tooling is far behind the brief's engine: the only Pons sniper on GitHub polls per-address tax over eth_call every 100 ms and broadcasts via plain RPC
findings.claim: Trustdev-eth/pons-sniper-bot-v1-v2 (TypeScript, 1 star, 0 forks, two commits both on 2026-09-08) subscribes to Pons factory logs over websocket, then for V2 polls 'effective buy tax for the trading address', expected output and price impact via eth_call every V2_TAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS (default 100 ms) and fires only when the address-specific opening tax is under a limit; it does a preflight eth_call, signs locally, supports multi-wallet with isolated nonce queues, TP/SL/trailing/timed exits, daily spend and loss caps, and its README admits no 'guaranteed block position or universal latency advantage' and ships an empty benchmark table. It does not read the sequencer feed, has no relay contract and no burst logic. The only Robinhood feed readers on GitHub are the two decoders above (Python 30 stars, Rust 5 stars), both read-only.
findings.relevance: Answers the survey question for this venue: the rival 'fleets' (400+ shots) are private code; nothing public explains their timing. The one reusable piece is the per-address effective-tax eth_call as a cheap sanity check that a shooter wallet is not accidentally 'named' or blacklisted before a burst.
findings.test: Clone and run in paper mode against the feed for an hour to confirm the feature list; add its per-address tax view call to the engine's pre-burst checks and compare with the surcharge actually paid on fills.

findings.title: Creator-side 'sell into the snipers' bots exist as open source; Pons V2's named-buyer exemption is the protocol version of the Solana create+buy bundle, so test whether named wallets dump inside the 11-block hold
findings.claim: jcoulaud/pumpfun-sniping-bot (TypeScript, 14 stars) is a creator-side bot: it creates a token, buys 70-80% of the wallet (cap 2 SOL, 5% slippage) in the same flow, watches over websocket and 'sells all tokens when someone else buys, or after timeout' (SELL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS default 20). Solana 'bundler' repos advertise create+buy with up to 20 wallets in one Jito bundle so the creator's wallets are the first holders. On Pons V2 the 97% creation-second tax exempts buyers named in the creation, which gives creators the same first-holder privilege without bundles; a visible E1 crowd of two or more fleets is their natural exit.
findings.relevance: Touches the exit and the crowd gate: if named/creator wallets sell within our 11-block hold on launches with a crowd, the fixed hold is selling into their dump rather than ahead of it, and 'creation names buyers' is a pre-tick signal (available before E1, unlike tick-block crowds).
findings.test: On the 696 qualifying launches, flag creations with a non-empty named-buyer list; measure fill P&L with vs without, and the block offset from E1 to the first sell by a named or creator wallet; if a large share sell inside 11 blocks, test a 'no named buyers' gate or a shorter hold on flagged launches. Check first that this was not one of the nine rejected gate signals.

findings.title: Nitro's nonce-gap hold is not a queue jump: a nonce-too-high tx is kept up to 1 s and spliced immediately behind its predecessor in the predecessor's block (verified), so it cannot pre-position a shot
findings.claim: Sequencer defaults: nonce-cache-size 1024, nonce-failure-cache-size 1024, nonce-failure-cache-expiry 1 s ('maximum amount of time to wait for a predecessor before rejecting a tx with nonce too high'); the pre-checker at strictness 20 does not reject nonce gaps (only strictness 30 does). In precheckNonces, when the predecessor tx is in the current batch the held successor is inserted as the very next item (nextQueueItem), i.e. same block, index = predecessor + 1; the postTxFilter path pushes it to txRetryQueue for the front of the next block only if it was cached by the post-execution path. Either way the predecessor still has to win the arrival race, so the successor gains no position. On expiry the sender gets the original nonce-too-high error.
findings.relevance: Rules out a tempting trick before engineering time is spent on it, and explains an operational hazard: a shooter wallet whose previous tx (e.g. its sell) has not been sequenced will have its next shot silently held up to 1 s and then rejected, which looks like a sequencer stall.
findings.test: Send nonce N+1 then, 300 ms later, nonce N from one wallet to the sequencer endpoint; confirm both land with N+1 at index N+1 in the same block. In the engine, assert per-wallet 'no pending tx' before assigning a shooter to a burst.

findings.title: What does not transfer from the Solana and EVM-mempool bots, and why
findings.claim: (1) Shred/pre-execution detection (D3AD-E reports creates at shred 0 of a 79-shred segment; RPC Fast: gRPC 5-20 ms plus 50-200 ms ShredStream lookahead) has no analog: Robinhood's feed is emitted after the sequencer has ordered and executed the block and there is no mempool, and Arbitrum's paid Fast Feed is Arbitrum One only. (2) Tips, Jito bundles, SWQoS provider tips and jitodontfront accounts (vvizardev adapter, 7 relayers; RPC Fast tip floors 10-50x around hot launches) do nothing under FCFS, where gas price only has to clear the base fee (see PGA finding for when this flips). (3) Mempool liquidity-add sniping and same-gas front-running (saantiaguilera/liquidity-sniper Go, 173 stars, last commit 2021-11-23; sszczep C++, 193 stars, unmaintained; Humancyyborg revm honeypot simulation) rely on a public mempool. (4) Pre-signing and gas-variant pregeneration (sszczep: 2.5x faster than signing) and sub-ms Rust paths (D3AD-E 5-7 us detect thread) attack a cost the engine already has at 3.8 ms for 35 shots, off the critical path. (5) Honeypot/rug scanners (GoPlus, honeypot.is, RugCheck; the AllenHark and RPC Fast guides) are irrelevant for a factory-deployed bonding-curve token held for 11 blocks. (6) Timeboost express lane (200 ms advantage) is not enabled on Robinhood. The multi-wallet 'swarm + trigger contract' in liquidity-sniper is the same design as the 35-wallet BuyOnce relay, so nothing new there either.
findings.relevance: Prevents re-spending effort on the rejected Rust/C++ rewrite and on Solana-specific plumbing; the only Solana ideas that survive are fan-out submission, lane-race measurement and process isolation (separate findings).
findings.test: None needed; each item is excluded by a venue property documented above (no mempool, FCFS, feed after execution, no Timeboost).

findings.title: Supply is tracking Pons V2 curve volume with elasticity ~1.5, and chain congestion has collapsed (DefiLlama daily series, pulled raw)
findings.claim: DefiLlama 'Pons V2' daily volume (USD): Sep 5 161.4M, Sep 6 173.1M (peak), Sep 15 77.9M, Sep 16 35.1M, Sep 21 56.0M, Sep 22 42.0M, Sep 23 38.3M, Sep 24 26.1M, Sep 25 25.4M, Sep 26 22.4M, Sep 27 20.8M, Sep 28 27.6M. Pons daily fees: Sep 5 $11.42M peak, Sep 21 $3.39M, Sep 27 $1.31M, Sep 28 $1.46M (7-day total $12.9M vs 30-day $144M). Robinhood Chain gas fees: Sep 4 $6.04M, Sep 21 $312K, Sep 26 $91K, Sep 27 $68K, i.e. gas per dollar of Pons volume fell from 3.9% (Sep 4) to 0.33% (Sep 27), a 12x drop in congestion. Your fills fell from 20-33/day (Sep 21-23, avg volume $45.4M) to 6-11/day (Sep 26-27, avg $21.6M): volume fell 2.1x, fills 3.1x, so fills scale like volume^1.5. Launchpad-wide volume was $399M on Sep 16, lowest since Aug 29, vs $600M+ days in early September. The Sep 29 gas-subsidy expiry only covered Robinhood Wallet transactions, which are 1-2% of chain volume, so it does not touch bot gas directly.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: supply of fireable launches fell from 20-33 to 6-11 a day. Hypothesis: fireable count is a convex function of Pons curve volume (crowded launches are the tail), so a daily volume series is a usable supply forecast and a regime kill-switch; and the 12x drop in gas-per-volume implies the 400+-shot congestion misses should now be rare, so the 4 s sequencer-hold regime may already be gone.
findings.test: Regress daily fireable-launch count (from the 696-launch backtest plus live days) on DefiLlama daily Pons V2 volume in log-log form; check the exponent (~1.5) and use the fitted curve to set expected fills/day. Separately count launches with 400+ rival shots per day for Sep 4-8 vs Sep 21-28 from the feed archive to confirm the congestion regime has thinned; the raw JSON is saved at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fomo-memebot/a7a59693-7c2d-5b6c-b7df-e43fdbe7d612/scratchpad/pdfwork/pons.json and ../pons_fees.json, ../rh_fees.json.

findings.title: Capacity can be computed exactly: the Pons V2 phantom quote reserve is 1.68 ETH, so a $200 stake pays ~4.5% buy premium plus ~5% exit discount from its own impact
findings.claim: Pons V2 docs: constant-product curve amountOut = in*reserveOut/(reserveIn+in); reserved tokens = supply * phantomQuote/(phantomQuote+threshold). Bitquery: 5/7 of supply sells on the curve, 2/7 is reserved; casatrick: graduation threshold 4.2 ETH for native-quoted launches. Solving 2/7 = p/(p+4.2) gives phantomQuote = 1.68 ETH (starting FDV 1.68 ETH, graduation FDV 20.58 ETH, 12.25x). For a buy of x ETH into a fresh curve the average fill premium over spot is x/1.68 and the post-buy spot moves (1+x/1.68)^2-1. At ETH $2,653 (Sep 28): $13 = 0.0049 ETH -> 0.29% premium (0.58% spot move); $50 -> 1.1%; $100 -> 2.2%; $200 = 0.0754 ETH -> 4.5% premium (9.2% spot move). On exit the average sell discount is roughly position/(reserve+position); with 0.2 ETH of crowd inflow and a $200 position grown 25% that is ~5%. Own impact therefore rises from ~0.6 points at $13 to ~9.5 points at $200 against a 16-25 point gross edge; break-even stake is roughly $300-350 if nothing else changes.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: stake is $13 because capacity is untested and the model says linear to $200. Hypothesis: the model is missing the constant-product own-impact term (or the phantom reserve is different from 1.68 ETH); the true capacity curve is concave and flattens well before $200.
findings.test: Read the active launch config from the factory (fields: supply, curveFeeBps, phantomQuote, graduationThreshold) to confirm phantomQuote = 1.68e18 wei for the ETH-quoted config; then replay the 130 modelled fills using getReserves()-exact math for stakes $13/$25/$50/$100/$200, inserting your buy and 11-block sell into the recorded flow, and plot net per fill versus stake. If the concavity holds, stake at the argmax of expected dollars per day rather than at $200.

findings.title: The 3-second tax window is a mutable owner setting; docs describe 5 s (E1 tax 24.75%) and the contract source defaults to 15 s (E1 99%), so the seat economics can change without notice
findings.claim: Formula: snipeTaxBps(elapsed) = snipeTaxStartBps >> ((elapsed*14)/snipeTaxSeconds). Live factory: snipeTaxStartBps = 9900, snipeTaxSeconds = 3 -> 99.00% / 6.18% / 0.19% / 0 (confirmed by casatrick, PumpDev's API doc and bodkin/dzo dry runs on Sep 3-4). Both values are owner-mutable via setters; getters snipeTaxStartBps() selector 0x50e25ac2 and snipeTaxSeconds() selector 0x6783774b. The public docs describe a 5 s window (~25% at 1 s, ~3% at 2 s), which under the formula is 24.75% / 3.09% / 0.38% / 0.04% / 0. pons-labs issue #10 (Sep 14) reports the checked-in factory source defaults to 15 seconds (99% / 49.5% / 24.75% / 12.4% / 6.19% / 3.09% ... 0 at 15 s) and that the published curve source lacks the anti-snipe view functions, i.e. the deployed bytecode is not the published source. Fee policy is snapshotted per launch, so a change applies to new launches only.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: fees take 36% of the gross move and the whole edge lives in the 6.18% E1 seat. Hypothesis: a parameter change to 5 s would raise the E1 surcharge to 24.75% and move the only viable seat to E2/E3 (3.09%/0.38%), killing the current rule; the risk is unpriced today.
findings.test: Poll both getters every minute and on every TokenLaunched, store the values with each launch, and hard-stop the engine when either changes; also verify per-launch by calling the curve's snipe-tax view (or reading SnipeTaxCharged on rival E1 buys) so the engine uses the snapshot, not the factory default. Backtest the 696 launches under the 5 s schedule to know in advance whether any seat survives.

findings.title: Robinhood Chain runs plain FCFS sequencing (no Timeboost), so second-place fills are pure latency and there is no priority to buy; enabling Timeboost would end that
findings.claim: Chainstack's feed decoder: the Robinhood Chain feed message carries no express-lane bitmap, 'no Timeboost: no express lane, no bidding your way to the front of a block'; one message = one 100 ms block; the chain averages ~71 tx/s. Timeboost is an opt-in setting for Orbit chains that imposes a 200 ms delay on non-express-lane transactions per 1-minute round; on Arbitrum One three entities win 99.74% of express-lane auctions (arXiv 2509.22143).
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: landing second costs 9 points and happens on ~40% of fills. Hypothesis: with FCFS the only lever is wire path and timing (already sub-ms in the engine), so the 40% is set by rivals' physical proximity to the sequencer, not by anything purchasable; conversely, if Robinhood turns on Timeboost, a non-controller cannot win E1 at all.
findings.test: Add a watcher on the feed message header for the express-lane field (the chainstack decoder exposes it) and on the ArbOwner/Timeboost config, and alert on change. Separately, measure the arrival-time distribution of the rivals that beat you (feed timestamp minus your send timestamp) to bound how much of the 40% is reachable by a shorter wire path versus not.

findings.title: Exemption-bundle launches ($15.5-18.4M extracted, 53-56 launches) put a curve-emptying buy 1-3 blocks after creation, inside your E1 window
findings.claim: Wazz (Sep 27): 53 Pons V2 launches Jul 10-Sep 21, $18.43M extracted (Bitquery's own count: 56 launches, $15.5M); The Block confirmed 10. Pattern: the creation transaction exempts 15-25 wallets (31 in EQUITY; the cap is 32), and 'one to three blocks later, a single transaction bought tokens for each one of them at once. In each launch, that single transaction emptied the bonding curve'; creator plus exempt wallets held 82-86% of supply; 25 of 53 launches used one bundling contract created Aug 28; DEED was funded 40 minutes before launch from DRAFT's 179.88 ETH sweep. Open-source Pons snipers (bodkin) refuse 'declared bundles (exempt wallets)' by default via a --max-exempt-wallets flag.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: launches that cannot be taken, second-place fills, and the minOut guard. Hypothesis: a launch whose creation names 15+ exempt wallets has a deterministic 4.2 ETH curve-emptying buy landing at block 1-3, which is before E1 for creations early in their second (your burst then reverts or buys the graduated pool at 12x) and after E1 for creations late in their second (you front-run the bundle and it graduates around you). Exemption-list length is readable in the creation itself, before the tick.
findings.test: Tag the 696 qualifying launches with the length of the creation's exempt address[] and with whether a buy >= 4.2 ETH landed within 3 blocks; split the 130 modelled fills and the 14 live fills by that tag and compare fill rate, revert rate, first-vs-second placement and net return. If this overlaps one of the nine rejected gate signals, at least report the split so the overlap is explicit.

findings.title: Every public Pons sniper tool targets the 0.19% window (E2), 1.2-1.7 s after detection, with $27-53 stakes; E1 rivals are closed fleets and your 11-block sell lands at the E2 boundary
findings.claim: dzo ('wait for zero'): polls tax every 150 ms and enters when it falls below an adaptive ceiling of 0.18-0.31%, observed 1.1-1.7 s after websocket detection; example buys 0.01-0.02 ETH, session budget 0.05 ETH, exits +80% / -35% / 25% trailing / 45 min max. bodkin: all dry-run and two live entries at exactly 0.19% tax, 1.2-1.6 s after detection; single wallet; launch-card reads take 279-284 ms. Trustdev bot: V2_MAX_EFFECTIVE_TAX_BPS=100 (1%), BUY_AMOUNT_ETH=0.01, MAX_DAILY_SPEND_ETH=0.10. PumpDev API: maxSnipeTaxBps ceiling, HTTP 425 if the tax is above tolerance. casatrick tells readers the optimal entry is 'the second window ... where the tax has decayed to near-zero'. Both terminals logged 24,462 launches and 559 graduations (2.3%) on Sep 3 and 56-152 launches per 5 minutes.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: the fixed 11-block hold and exit liquidity. Hypothesis (explanatory, not a new exit rule): your sell at E1+1.1 s falls 1.2-2.1 s after creation, i.e. just before or at the start of the 0.19% second, so the buyers you sell into are the tail of the 6.18% payers plus the first 'wait for zero' bots; if that public-tool population thins with volume, realized exit slippage rises even when the gross move is unchanged (live +7.6% vs modelled +16.1%).
findings.test: From the feed archive, count per launch the buys whose SnipeTaxCharged is ~19 bps (E2 entrants) and ~618 bps (E1 rivals) for Sep 4-8 vs Sep 21-28; regress your realized sell slippage on the E2 count in the sell block +/-2; track the daily E2-entrant count as an exit-liquidity gauge alongside the two-fleet gate.

findings.title: When a launchpad's volume halves, its professional sniper population does not halve, it fires less: pump.fun evidence and a 13-day census of 1,012 persistent sniper cohorts
findings.claim: pump.fun Jan->Feb 2025: volume -63%, graduations -80% (about 1,200/day on Jan 23-24 to about 200 by Feb 26). Kamat (arXiv 2607.02795, Jun 11-25 2026, 166,098 launches = 12,400/day, 1,578,333 buyer events): 1,012 persistent cohorts from 2,965 addresses; median cohort 2 wallets (56.4% pairs); only 22 cohorts hit >= 20 launches in 13.4 days; the top cohort (9 wallets) hit 42 launches in 11 days (3.8/day) at mean first-buyer rank 2.29 committing 68.12 SOL (1.6 SOL per launch); 5,419 launches (3.3%) had a persistent cohort among the first 10 buyers; cohort presence lifts 30-minute buyer count by +16.1% but SOL inflow only +6.3% (not significant). jmenzler's bot-anticipation strategy: per-attempt losses of 0.01-0.3 SOL replaced a high-win-rate distribution within ~3 months as the sniper cohort's filters evolved through ~8 stages and the author fell off the speed frontier.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: the two-fleet gate fires on fewer launches as volume falls. Hypothesis: professional fleets are few (tens of cohorts) and selective (a few launches per day each), so their co-occurrence on the same launch drops faster than volume, which is exactly the volume^1.5 relation in finding 1; the fleets are still present and will re-crowd launches when volume returns, so this is a dormancy problem, not an exit problem.
findings.test: Fingerprint rival fleets on the feed (shared funding, shot spacing, wallet counts) and count distinct fleets per day and shots per fleet per day for Sep 4-8 vs Sep 21-28; if fleet count is flat and shots-per-fleet fell, supply will recover with volume and the engine should idle rather than loosen the gate.

findings.title: Public operators size $50-300 per shot and scale P&L by trade count, not stake: pump.fun retrospective (7 -> ~1,000 SOL), Clanker v4.0 auction data, RPC Fast slot economics
findings.claim: jmenzler (Feb-Apr 2024): starting capital 7 SOL to ~1,000 SOL (~143x) over ~3 months; per-trade notional 0.6-2 SOL; ~50 trades/day, ~5,000 trades, ~2,500 round trips; peak working capital on the hot wallet ~100 SOL; effectively no losing days until the terminal decay window. Clanker v4.0 (30 days, 52,612 coins): 245 sniper auctions (0.47% of coins), 14 unique auction participants, average winning bid 0.025 ETH (~$100), highest ~0.07 ETH (~$300); block 2-3 swaps averaged 7% of supply, block 10 swaps 1%. RPC Fast (vendor): slot 0 vs slot 2 is 20-60% of upside on pump.fun; co-located sub-35 ms lands slot 0 in ~89% of events vs <20% at 220 ms; a client at median entry slot 3.2 with 31% bundle acceptance had profit per attempt near zero after fees; roughly 90% of DIY sniper bots fail.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: stake untested above $13 and the 9-point first-vs-second gap. Hypothesis: the best-documented operator ran ~50 trades/day at ~$100-300 each, consistent with the concave capacity in finding 2; growth came from breadth (more launches, more venues) rather than depth, and the second-place cost you measured (9 points) sits inside the 20-60%-of-upside range others report.
findings.test: Compare dollars/day at stake S from the finding-2 replay against the alternative of widening breadth (more hours online, the E1-plus-crowd launches you currently skip at small size, LONG/pools.trade per finding 10); also compute your per-shot gas at today's gas (chain fees fell 99%) to see whether the 35-shot burst is now cheap enough to fire on marginal launches.

findings.title: No other live venue reproduces the 3-second exponential tax; on Robinhood Chain the only other launchpad with real volume is LONG (Doppler Multicurve, ~25% of launchpad volume, no time tax)
findings.claim: Same chain: LONG (long.xyz) launches through Doppler Airlock 0xeb7c034704ef8dcd2d32324c1545f62fb4ad0862 with Doppler Multicurve v4 pools paired to stock tokens (NVDA, AAPL, MSFT, GOOGL, TSLA, MU, SPCX); ~25% of the $600M launchpad volume on Sep 1 and ~$100M in its first month; anti-snipe is a 24-hour ticker reservation, no time tax. pools.trade: v4 pool from block one, creator buys in the launch block, 0.25% LP fee, no launchpad fee, no tax, 'thousands per day at peak' but ~$38K/day fees in late August vs Pons $4.9M. PAIR: caps of 5.5% per buy and 5.0% per wallet for the launch block plus 5 blocks, 1% swap fee, $26M cumulative volume over 1,200 tokens. Pons V1: only the creator's buy executes in the launch block, 5% wallet cap for 2 blocks. Clanker on Robinhood Chain: $457/day fees (Base $30.7K/day) with 80%->5% parabolic fee decay over 30 s. Other chains: Zora TrendCoins on Base 99% -> 0.01% linear over 10 s, but DefiLlama Zora fees are $138-1,126/day in September (dead); Meteora DBC on Solana has a fee scheduler (e.g. 50% -> 1% over 120 s in 40 steps) on a different stack. Bitquery also lists Virtuals, Flap.sh, Klik, Ape.store, Bags.fm as active Robinhood Chain launch factories, all without time-based taxes.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: supply. Hypothesis: the engine's edge (fleet detection on the feed plus timed burst) is portable only to a venue with a crowd that fires at a predictable block; LONG and pools.trade launches have no tax, so the seat is block N+1 after creation with 0.25-1% fees instead of 8.9%, but only if rival fleets crowd them. Nothing off-chain is worth the port at current volumes.
findings.test: Point the existing feed listener at the Doppler Airlock and the pools.trade entry contract (0x0000ffffbe8efe702c8703ae3477ff5de3d319c0) for one week; for each launch count buyers in blocks +1..+10, repeated fleet signatures, and the price move from block +1 to +12; if a two-fleet crowd appears on >= 10 launches/day with a positive post-fee move at 0.25-1% fees, run the same burst there in shadow mode.

findings.title: Base rates for Pons V2 launches (Bitquery, Aug 3-Sep 3): 79.6% trade at all, 38.6% reach 5 buyers, 1.55% graduate, half of graduations within 4 minutes, and half of active wallets on the peak day were first-timers
findings.claim: 207,893 coins in 32 days; 165,446 (79.6%) traded at least once; 80,317 (38.6%) found 5+ buyers; 3,228 (1.55%) graduated, half within 4 minutes; $736M traded on curves vs $2.14B after graduation; busiest day Sep 3 $517M; on Sep 3, 35,008 of 69,598 wallets that traded a Pons coin had never traded one before (50.3%). Datawallet: 19,541 launches on Sep 2, 53,555 over Sep 1-3, gas ~$0.40/tx at peak congestion. Bitquery exposes SnipeTaxCharged per buy and per-launch buyer counts via its API.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: supply concentration by hour and the fall in fireable launches. Hypothesis: the crowd's fuel is new-wallet inflow (half the active wallets were new on the peak day); daily new-wallet count is a leading indicator of fireable launches that is available from Bitquery without touching the feed.
findings.test: Pull daily distinct first-time Pons traders from Bitquery for Sep 1-28 and correlate with daily fireable launches and with the 16:00-24:00 UTC share; if the correlation beats DefiLlama volume alone, use it as the supply forecast.

findings.title: The Robinhood Chain gas subsidy that ended Sep 29 covered only Robinhood Wallet transactions (1-2% of chain volume); flow is routed by terminals (GMGN 4.86M swaps / $947.5M over Sep 1-3) charging 0.5-1%
findings.claim: 90-day rebate from Jul 1 for transactions sent from the Robinhood Wallet, threshold cut from $5.00 to $0.50 in mid-August, expired Sep 29; the Robinhood app accounts for 'one to two percent' of chain trading volume; 'most of the fee-generating activity ... runs through the memecoin launchpad Pons and through trading bots'. GMGN handled 4.86M swaps and $947.5M routed volume on Sep 1-3, more than Axiom, OKX, Maestro and the gasless account-abstraction stack combined; terminals charge 0.5-1% per trade. Datawallet's own threshold: DEX volume under $200M/day after the subsidy would indicate subsidy dependence.
findings.relevance: Bottleneck: supply and the crowd's composition. Hypothesis: the subsidy end is not a mechanical hit to the crowd (the crowd pays its own gas through GMGN/Axiom) but the terminals' 0.5-1% fee plus 6.18% E1 tax means the E1 crowd is paying ~7-9% to be in your seat, so their presence is a strong commitment signal; watch terminal volume, not Robinhood app volume, for supply.
findings.test: Track Pons V2 daily volume (finding 1) and terminal-routed volume for Sep 29-Oct 6 against the prior week; if volume does not break lower after the subsidy end, the late-September decline is memecoin-cycle driven and mean-reverts with attention rather than with gas policy.
